title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

title: Synergistic functions of copper-based nanomaterials modified granular activated carbon: antibacterial activity, antibiotics adsorption, and impact of preceding chlorination on antibiotic resistance genes removal in tertiary treated hospital effluents
abstract: The synergistic efficacy and mechanisms of antibacterial activity and adsorption of antibiotics/intermediates using copper-based nanomaterials modified granular activated carbon (GAC) were evaluated, including the impact of preceding chlorination on the reduction of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) in effluents treated by fixed-bed column. Copper-based MOFs coated on GACs (GAC-CuBDC and GAC-CuNHBDC) exhibited higher antibacterial efficacy than the functionalized GACs (-COOH and -NH) and copper oxide (CuO and CuO)-coated GACs, which 100% eliminated both Gram-negativeand Gram-positivebacteria (5.5 and 5.1 log reduction, respectively). Notably, GAC-CuBDC can inhibit the growth of total bacteria and presumptivein the matrix of hospital effluents to non-detectable levels; however, interference from dissolved organic matter in the effluents can reduce antibacterial efficacy, requiring an increased solid-to-liquid ratio from 4 to 8 g/L to achieve 100% inhibition. Hydrophilic GAC-CuBDC exhibited high performance in adsorbing intermediates derived from penicillin G, ampicillin, ceftazidime, and ciprofloxacin. The intermediates found in chlorinated effluent could be more easily eliminated by functionalized GACs than those in non-chlorinated effluent. The adsorption capacities of penicillin G, ceftazidime, and ciprofloxacin onto GAC-CuBDC were comparable to those of pristine GAC, whereas ampicillin showed a two-fold higher adsorption on GAC-CuBDC than on pristine GAC. Adsorption mechanisms of antibiotics onto GAC-CuBDC may include hydrogen bonding and π-π interactions (involving -NH and nitroaromatic ring of the antibiotic) with the acidic functional groups of GAC, combined with hydrogen bonding at the terminal -OH groups of the CuBDC copper nodes. Passage through the fixed-bed column of GAC-CuBDC could reduce the intracellular ARGs and ARB from hospital effluents. However, the coexistence of chlorination may promote the growth ofand interfere with the reduction of some ARGs and ARB after tertiary treatment by the GAC-CuBDC column. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40201-026-01007-w.

title: Photocatalytic degradation of ciprofloxacin in water using BiOCl/Bi(2)S(3) composite: Experimental and model-predicted kinetic evaluation
abstract: Pharmaceutical contaminants in wastewater pose a significant environmental and public health risks. The conventional treatment methods often used suffer from incomplete degradation, high costs, and limited applicability. To address these shortcomings, this study developed an efficient visible-light-driven photocatalytic degradation of pharmaceutical contaminants particularly antibiotics which contributes significantly to environmental pollution. A novel BiOCl/BiSphotocatalyst was synthesized through a facile one-step method to enhance charge separation and suppress electron-hole recombination. The research used ciprofloxacin antibiotic as a model pollutant. The innovative aspect of this work lies in tuning the BiOCl: BiSmole ratios (3:1, 5:1, 7:1) to identify the optimal configuration for maximum degradation efficiency under visible light and found that 5:1 BiOCl/BiSachieved 94% of ciprofloxacin (CIP) degradation within 50 min under 300 W visible irradiation. Systematic optimization of pH, catalyst dosage, and initial concentration was also studied. The degradation pathway was elucidated through intermediate analysis, while kinetic studies using both linear and nonlinear Langmuir-Hinshelwood models confirmed the enhanced reactivity. This study also integrates computational kinetic modeling with experimental data using polynomial fit and showed the nonlinear relationship of predicted and experimental kinetic constants with different initial concentration of CIP. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40201-026-01008-9.

Staphylococcus aureus in bovine intramammary infections: A global systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence and antimicrobial resistance patterns
abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

abstract: Mastitis is a multifactorial disease with major consequences for production, animal welfare, and public health, yet it remains less studied in goats than in cows. Moreover, reports of antimicrobial resistance among bacteria isolated from mastitic goats are scarce. In Ethiopia, treatment decisions for mastitis largely rely on empirical clinical experience rather than routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted from November to December 2024 in Waghimra, Amhara, Ethiopia, to identify the major bacterial causes of mastitis and to evaluate their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. Bacterial isolation, identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing followed standard protocols, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 17 and WHONET software. The overall goat-level mastitis prevalence was 24.69% (98/397), comprising 2.52% (10/397) clinical and 22.28% (88/395) subclinical mastitis.spp. (47/129; 36.43%) was the predominant isolate, followed by(12/129; 9.30%) andspp. (3/129; 2.33%). Allisolates were resistant to ampicillin (37/37; 100%) and showed considerable resistance to tetracycline (16/37; 43.24%), but remained highly susceptible to kanamycin (36/37; 97.30%), chloramphenicol, and gentamicin (35/37; 94.59% each).andspp. were highly susceptible to most antimicrobials tested, except ampicillin. Multidrug resistance was detected in 13.46% (7 out of 52) of isolates, occurring exclusively amongspp. Subclinical mastitis, mainly caused byspp., was highly prevalent in the study area, showing complete ampicillin resistance and considerable tetracycline resistance. Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Harnessing hydrogel technology for advanced periodontitis therapy: A multifunctional approach to oral health restoration
abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: Extraction of chondroitin sulfate from chicken cartilage by Bacillus velezensis 259 fermentation: whole-genome analysis and process optimization
abstract: This study used chicken cartilage as the raw material and employed microbial fermentation with259 (259) to extract chondroitin sulfate (CS). The CS extraction rate served as the primary evaluation index to investigate the effects of bacterial inoculation amount, cartilage addition amount, and fermentation time on extraction efficiency. First,259 was evaluated for its gelatinolytic and proteolytic activities and safety-related characteristics, followed by whole-genome analysis to investigate its genomic features and the presence of potential virulence and antimicrobial resistance genes. Subsequently, single-factor experiments and response surface optimization were conducted. A quadratic polynomial model was established using the Box-Behnken design, and response surface analysis was performed to determine the optimal process parameters for CS extraction from fermented chicken cartilage using259. The results showed that the optimal extraction conditions were 6.2% inoculation amount, 22.5% cartilage addition amount, 37 °C, 180 r/min and 20.8 h fermentation time. Under these conditions, the CS extraction rate reached 17.9%. In addition, UV and Raman spectroscopy further showed that the crude CS extract exhibited spectral characteristics similar to those of the CS-A and CS-C standards. These findings demonstrated the feasibility of using259 fermentation for CS extraction from chicken cartilage and provided optimized process parameters for this approach. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-026-05101-6.

An in Silico Characterisation of ATP-Binding Cassette Transporter Proteins Across Five Endodontic Pathogens: Implications for Antimicrobial Resistance and Virulence
abstract: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter proteins play pivotal roles in antimicrobial resistance and bacterial virulence. However, their characterisation across major endodontic pathogens remains limited. This study aimed to characterise ABC transporter proteins in silico across five endodontic pathogens and to investigate their implications for antimicrobial resistance and virulence. Reference genome-predicted proteomes of Enterococcus faecalis, Porphyromonas gingivalis, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Actinomyces naeslundii and Dialister invisus were retrieved from the National Center for Biotechnology Information RefSeq database. ABC transporter proteins were identified using InterProScan and HMMER and assigned to five functional categories based on Pfam domain signatures. Physicochemical parameters were computed and analysed by principal component analysis, the Kruskal-Wallis test and the chi-square test of independence. Domain architecture and phylogenetic analyses were performed using MAFFT, FastTree and Interactive Tree of Life. A total of 574 ABC transporter proteins were identified (range: 63-168 per species), with A. naeslundii exhibiting the highest transporter density (55.3 per Mb). Putative multidrug resistance pumps were dominant (78.7%) and were highest in F. nucleatum (87.1%) and E. faecalis (82.2%). Functional category distribution differed significantly between species (χ = 22.043, df = 8, p = 0.005). Significant inter-species differences were identified in Grand Average of Hydropathy (GRAVY) score, aromaticity, isoelectric point and instability index (all p < 0.001). BLASTP confirmed the efrAB efflux operon in E. faecalis (EfrA: 99.65%; EfrB: 100.00%) alongside 13 homologue proteins. The dominance of putative multidrug resistance pumps, including sequence-confirmed efrAB proteins and 13 homologues in E. faecalis, provides a plausible molecular framework for intrinsic resistance to intracanal medicaments in persistent endodontic infections.

title: Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Program, 1 January to 31 March 2026
abstract: The Australian National Neisseria Network (NNN) comprises reference laboratories in each state and territory that report data on antimicrobial susceptibility testing to an agreed group of antimicrobial agents for the Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme (AGSP). The AGSP data are presented quarterly in tabulated form, as well as in the AGSP annual report. This report presents national gonococcal antimicrobial resistance surveillance data from 1 January to 31 March 2026.

title: Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme Annual Report, 2025
abstract: The Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme (AGSP) has continuously monitored antimicrobial resistance in(NG) for more than 45 years through the system of jurisdictionalreference laboratories, the National Neisseria Network (NNN). In 2025, a total of 10,204 isolates across Australia, from public and private sectors, were tested for in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility by standardised methods. In 2025, the AGSP captured antimicrobial susceptibility data for 23.9% of all gonococcal infection notifications nationally. The current treatment recommendation for gonorrhoea, for the majority of Australia, continues to be dual therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. In 2025, of NG isolates tested, 0.73% (74/10,204) met the World Health Organization (WHO) criterion for decreased susceptibility (DS) to ceftriaxone, defined as a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) ≥ 0.125 mg/L. This proportion of isolates meeting the ceftriaxone DS criterion was greater than that reported in 2024 (0.51%), with the majority from New South Wales and Victoria. Genomic analysis indicated that 64.9% of these isolates (48/74) possessed the mosaic penA 60.001 allele, the key target associated with ceftriaxone resistance. Resistance to azithromycin was reported in 7.1% of NG isolates nationally, increasing from being proportionally stable (3.9% to 4.7%) since 2019. Of NG isolates tested, 0.20% (20/10,204) exhibited high-level resistance to azithromycin (MIC value ≥ 256 mg/L), with cases reported across Australia, predominantly in New South Wales, Victoria and non-remote Western Australia. There were ten isolates detected in 2025 that had an extensively drug-resistant (XDR) phenotype: i.e., displaying both high-level resistance to azithromycin and decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone (MIC ≥ 0.125 mg/L). When added to the 14 XDR isolates reported during 2022-2024, this brings the total to 24 XDR NG isolates reported in Australia since 2022. Genomic analyses of the ten XDR isolates reported in 2025 indicated all harboured the mosaic penA 60.001 allele, with several differing sequence types (ST) identified. By contrast, during 2022 and 2024, XDR NG sequence types were limited to ST-16406, consistent with reports from Europe and England. Travel information, where available, indicates infections in 2025 were associated with travel to Southeast Asia but also arose where no travel was involved. In 2025, penicillin resistance was found in 23.4% of gonococcal isolates, and ciprofloxacin resistance in 59.3% of isolates where tested, although there was variation by jurisdiction particularly in remote settings, where acquisition of cultures for antimicrobial susceptibility testing is low. Tetracycline resistance has been included in surveillance in the AGSP in recent years, coincident with increasing use of doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis for syphilis and chlamydia. Nationally 36.2% of NG isolates in 2025 were tetracycline resistant, with variation by jurisdiction. No isolates were resistant to spectinomycin; data for gentamicin, whilst no breakpoints are defined, are reported by the AGSP as these data are reportable to the WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS). The emergence of antimicrobial resistant NG in Australia has largely occurred through importation, spread and local transmission. In 2025, in Australia and overseas, increased detection of drug-resistant NG isolates is of significant concern as the threat for the future of the current recommended therapeutic agents is increasingly evident, and no ideal alternate therapeutic agent has been identified. Disease prevention strategies under investigation for the future have included the MenB-4C vaccine, designed to protect against meningococcal disease. Despite early promise, recent results from a large Australian trial indicate the MenB-4C vaccine is not effective at preventing gonorrhoea in men who are at high risk of infection. The AGSP continues to monitor antimicrobial resistance and to identify emerging resistant clones by enhanced surveillance approaches, to inform strategies for disease management and treatment of gonorrhoea in Australia.

title: What are people saying about DoxyPEP? A topic-based analysis of Reddit discussions
Antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of ZnO-NPs against Streptococcus suis serotype 9 in vitro
abstract: is an important swine pathogen and an emerging zoonotic threat, with serotype 9 (SS9) increasingly recognized as an important pathogenic serotype. Biofilm formation contributes to the persistence, antimicrobial tolerance, and pathogenicity of, yet effective strategies for controlling biofilm-associated infections caused by SS9 remain limited. In this study, we evaluated the antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) against SS9 and investigated whether their effects were associated with oxidative stress, biofilm formation, and alterations in virulence-associated genes. The minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum biofilm eradication concentration of ZnO-NPs against SS9 were both 49 μg/mL. ZnO-NPs exhibited potent antibacterial and antibiofilm activities, significantly inhibiting biofilm formation and reducing biofilm viability in a dose-dependent manner. Crystal violet staining demonstrated a marked reduction in biofilm biomass, while SEM analysis revealed substantial disruption of bacterial morphology and biofilm architecture following ZnO-NPs treatment. In addition, ZnO-NPs markedly increased intracellular reactive oxygen species levels, indicating the induction of oxidative stress in SS9. ZnO-NPs treatment also reduced the major extracellular matrix components of the biofilm, including extracellular proteins and extracellular DNA. Furthermore, RT-qPCR analysis showed that ZnO-NPs downregulated the expression of biofilm- and virulence-associated genes, including,,, and. Collectively, these findings indicate that ZnO-NPs exert antibacterial and antibiofilm effects against SS9, accompanied by oxidative stress induction, disruption of biofilm architecture and extracellular matrix, and modulation of biofilm- and virulence-associated genes. ZnO-NPs may, therefore, represent a promising candidate for controlling SS9-associated infections.IMPORTANCEserotype 9 (SS9) is an important pathogen associated with disease in pigs and represents a potential zoonotic threat. The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance highlights the need for alternative approaches to control SS9 infections. In this study, zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) showed antibacterial and antibiofilm activity against SS9, including disruption of established biofilms. These findings provide evidence for further exploring ZnO-NPs as a non-antibiotic strategy for controlling SS9 infections and support future studies evaluating their safety and efficacy in animals.

title: Large-Scale Comparative Genomics of 1,374 Lactiplantibacillus plantarum Genomes Reveals an Open Pan-genome and Strain-Level Variation in Probiotic-Associated and Safety-Related Genomic Features
abstract: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum is widely studied for food fermentation and probiotic applications, but its functional and safety-related characteristics are strongly strain dependent. Large-scale comparative genomics can characterize this diversity and support genome-informed strain prioritization, although genomic evidence alone does not establish probiotic efficacy or safety. A RefSeq genome collection of L. plantarum was subjected to accession-level auditing, exact-sequence dereplication, and predefined genome-quality filtering, yielding 1,374 unique genomes for final analysis. Genome characteristics, pan-genome structure, probiotic-associated annotation proxies, targeted sequence evidence, predefined safety-related genomic markers, isolation-source metadata, and COG functional annotations were evaluated. The final cohort had a mean genome size of 3.286 ± 0.126 Mb and a mean GC content of 44.419 ± 0.168%. Genome size and GC content showed a negative dataset-level association (Pearson's r = - 0.767; R = 0.588). The observed pan-genome comprised 32,500 gene families, including 1,175 core and 31,325 accessory families, and remained non-saturating, with a Heaps' law exponent of γ = 0.289. Probiotic-associated annotation proxies showed heterogeneous prevalence, and targeted sequence analysis demonstrated that annotation nomenclature could substantially influence apparent marker detection. Evidence-supported antibiotic-resistance markers were detected in 46 genomes (3.35%) and mobile-genetic-element-associated markers in 93 (6.77%), whereas ldhD was detected in 1,372 genomes (99.85%). The predefined descriptive concern score assigned 1,236 genomes (90.0%) to the Lowest Genomic Concern category, 136 (9.9%) to the Low category, and two (0.1%) to the Moderate category. Only 1,327 of the 32,500 gene families received a recognized primary COG assignment. The quality-filtered L. plantarum RefSeq collection exhibits an open, accessory-rich pan-genome and substantial strain-level genomic diversity. Annotation-dependent marker detection, uneven database representation, and the limited discrimination of the descriptive concern score emphasize that genome-based screening should be used for candidate prioritization rather than as evidence of probiotic efficacy or definitive safety. Strain-specific phenotypic and application-relevant safety validation remains essential.

title: Molecular Detection Technologies for Helicobacter pylori Antibiotic Resistance: Current Status and Clinical Implications
abstract: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infects approximately half of the global population and is closely linked to chronic gastritis, peptic ulcers, and gastric cancer. Antibiotic resistance has become a major global health concern with marked regional variations, severely undermining empirical treatment efficacy. Resistance mechanisms primarily involve target gene mutations, efflux pump overexpression, and altered membrane permeability. This review summarizes resistance mechanisms of commonly used antibiotics against H. pylori, along with diagnostic approaches ranging from phenotypic to molecular methods, the latter offering faster and more precise mutation detection, yet limited by high costs and invasive sampling. Treatment has shifted from clarithromycin-based triple therapy to bismuth-containing quadruple and potassium-competitive acid blocker-based regimens. However, susceptibility-guided therapy faces implementation barriers, and empirical regimens remain prevalent. Future directions emphasize affordable multiplex molecular platforms, resistance surveillance networks, artificial intelligence-driven predictive models, and non-antibiotic adjunctive strategies. Integrating molecular diagnostics with antimicrobial stewardship to transition from empirical to precision-based management is critical for improving eradication rates and curbing further resistance spread.

title: Nano-kinetic implant surface mediates osteo-antibacterial synergy through electromagnetic-mechanical coupling
abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a devastating complication of total joint arthroplasty, mainly caused by bacterial biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance. Traditional static surfaces rely on contact killing-based bactericidal properties and cannot reliably clear mature biofilms. In this study, we fabricate a remote-activated dynamic biomimetic system, namely a movable magnetic topographic surface (MMTS). Here we show that under the exposure of external electromagnetic field (EMF), the anchored Janus nano-heterodimers oscillate periodically to mechanically disrupt bacterial membranes and eradicates biofilms of Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. This mechanical force can also activates Piezo1 mechanosensitive ion channel in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), inducing calcium oscillations, upregulating gene expression of Runx2 and BMP2, and enhancing extracellular matrix mineralization. In vivo, MMTS combined with EMF exposure eliminates local infection and promoted osseointegration. This remote-activated dynamic biomimetic strategy offers a promising multifunctional platform for PJI treatment, and improved implant osteointegration in clinical orthopedics.

title: Knowledge, attitudes and practices towards antibiotic prescription by veterinarians: A systematic review of qualitative studies
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a public health problem with global impacts. Thus, responsible antibiotic use across human and veterinary health sectors must be fostered. Veterinarians play a crucial role in antimicrobial stewardship (AMS), yet their prescribing attitudes are influenced by a complex interplay of factors. This study aimed to collect and synthesize evidence from qualitative studies focusing on the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of veterinarians regarding antibiotic prescription to identify the factors influencing clinical decisions and contribute to AMS strategies. This systematic review followed PRISMA and ENTREQ guidelines, with a protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024529868). On 15 March 2024, the databases Medline/PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Knowledge, and CAB International were searched without time restrictions, and an updated search was conducted on September 11, 2025. Only qualitative and mixed methods studies involving veterinarians working with companion or food-producing animals were included. Critical appraisal was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for qualitative research. After search and screening, 28 studies were included, with data mostly being collected through interviews. In total, 34 influencing factors were identified: intrinsic (n = 12) and extrinsic factors (n = 22). Among the intrinsic factors, professional experience, the need to satisfy client's expectations, fear of clinical complications, and fear of losing clients were the most identified. Among the extrinsic factors, client-related (financial resources, expectations, and compliance), antibiotic characteristics, disease prevention, and animal clinical status were identified as main drivers for antibiotic selection and prescribing. Larger-scale mixed methods or longitudinal studies, especially in underrepresented regions, should be encouraged. Strategies under the One Health approach should be effectively implemented to promote the rational use of antibiotics in veterinary medicine, integrating continuing education, easily accessible, practical, and updated regulatory policies and guidelines, animal facilities improvement, and programs that strengthen communication between veterinarians and animal owners.

title: Modern Sample Pretreatment Approaches for β-Lactam Antibiotics in Complex Matrices: Challenges and Innovations
abstract: β-lactam antibiotics, widely used in human and veterinary medicine, can trigger serious public health concerns through misuse-including antimicrobial resistance and drug residues. The detection of β-lactam antibiotics faces three challenges: unstable β-lactam rings prone to hydrolysis, complex metabolism requiring multi-residue analysis, and trace-level concentrations (μg/kg) with severe matrix interference demanding high sensitivity and accuracy. Thus, systematically optimizing sample analytical methods is essential to enhance monitoring programs and ensure food safety. This review offers a comprehensive overview of contemporary pretreatment methodologies, encompassing well-established techniques such as solid-phase extraction and dispersive liquid-liquid microextraction, as well as innovative approaches including solidification floating organic droplet liquid-liquid microextraction and electromembrane extraction. Recent advancements in pretreatment strategies for β-lactam antibiotics are increasingly oriented toward achieving high extraction and purification efficiency, enhancing environmental sustainability, and improving the reusability of extraction materials. By critically evaluating the advantages and limitations of various techniques, this review aims to support progress in detection accuracy and reliability, increase analytical throughput and efficiency, and reduce operational costs.

title: Fleming Fund Implementation in Kenya: What Have We Learned About Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance for Decision-making?
abstract: Kenya has moved from fragmented, pilot-based antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance toward a coordinated One Health system, and its experience, pathways of change, and remaining gaps are relevant for other low- and middle-income settings working to operationalize One Health AMR surveillance. Here, we report a narrative overview of programmatic learning using 2018 as the pre-Fleming Fund baseline, drawing on national and global surveillance reports, monitoring frameworks from the Quadripartite indicators, qualitative evidence on governance, implementation and policy evolution across the One Health sectors, and Fleming Fund documentation. Since 2018, AMR surveillance expanded from 2 human health sites to 30 human, animal, and environmental sites by 2025. National reports evolved to integrate AMR, antimicrobial consumption, and antimicrobial use data; routine reporting to global platforms matured; and outputs such as dashboards, reports, and policy briefs informing stewardship, Infection Prevention and Control, regulatory action, and policy decisions. External benchmarks showed improvement in AMR-related capacity, with World Health Organization Joint External Evaluation scores moving from limited to demonstrated capacity for surveillance and multisectoral coordination. Kenya's experience suggests that sustainable progress depends on embedding AMR surveillance within government-led governance structures, technical systems, and coordinated partner support, but sustaining gains will require predictable financing and routine data use.

title: Reflections for the Future of AMR Surveillance and AMR Action
abstract: This paper builds on the other papers in this series to present high-level lessons learnt and considerations for the future of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance and its contribution to action on AMR in low- and middle-income countries. Participatory synthesis involved engagement with individuals who had worked within and alongside the Fleming Fund from a range of organizations and geographies, to scope and solidify lessons learnt and future considerations relevant to a wide range of donors, partners, and policy makers or implementors. Contributors were invited to join a Writing Group, which included individuals from academia, clinical sciences, applied public, animal, environment, and food sciences health, as well as senior scientists and administrators from 14 organizations. The synthesis was informed by contributions to 4 virtual workshops and 3 drafts of the manuscript. Authors read and commented on the drafts, several wrote and referenced sections, and all gave substantive feedback with their reactions to the draft conclusions as consensus was built. Over nearly 10 years, the Fleming Fund achieved significant improvements in AMR surveillance. Analysis of the barriers and enablers across settings and systems highlights key lessons for how surveillance is positioned, funded, used, and innovated upon. The success of future AMR surveillance and its sustainability relies on planning within resource constraints for a sharpened system that focuses the scope, frequency, and depth of data to inform action, technical, and architectural developments directions to streamline investment and financing that supports country-led sustainable approaches. Investment in AMR surveillance and broader AMR actions has yielded substantial progress. Expanded domestic public financing, large-scale private sector engagement, or enhanced multilateral support will be needed to ensure recent gains are sustained. Progress will require well-designed, targeted, and cost-effective investments to maintain current capacity while enabling further system strengthening.

title: The Fleming Fund: Key Features of Design and Approach to Strengthening Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
abstract: This paper examines the Fleming Fund as a major long-term investment in strengthening antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance in low- and middle-income countries. Established by the UK Department of Health and Social Care in 2015, the Fund committed up to £498 million to support surveillance capacity across 25 countries in Africa and Asia through a One Health approach spanning human, animal and environmental health. The paper situates the Fleming Fund within wider global concern about AMR and highlights surveillance as essential for stewardship, policy and international coordination. It describes the Fleming Fund's design logic, governance arrangements, grant architecture and evolving strategic priorities, with particular attention to how the program combined laboratory strengthening, workforce development, data systems, quality assurance, sampling pathways and multisectoral coordination to generate credible and usable AMR data. The analysis also examines the Phase 2 shift from an initial emphasis on data generation toward greater attention to data interpretation, dissemination and use in policy and practice. Drawing on program documentation, evaluation evidence and stakeholder perspectives, the paper presents the Fleming Fund as an important case of large-scale surveillance system strengthening in resource-constrained settings. It argues that the Fund offers wider lessons on the time, coordination and institutional embedding required to move from externally supported capacity building toward sustainable national surveillance functions. These lessons are relevant to future AMR investments and to broader debates on global health security, health systems strengthening and One Health implementation.

title: Generating Actionable Data From Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance: Insights From the Fleming Fund's International Experience
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, with the greatest burden falling on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) also challenged with limited surveillance capacity. The UK Government's Fleming Fund was established in 2015 to strengthen AMR surveillance across Africa and Asia through a One Health approach. This paper draws on program experience, country implementation evidence, and published literature to describe how the Fleming Fund operationalized AMR surveillance, assess its contribution to the quantity and quality of surveillance data, identify key implementation challenges, and consider implications for future global surveillance strategies. The Fleming Fund combined investments in laboratory infrastructure, workforce development, quality assurance, data systems, governance, and data use. Across supported countries, these investments enabled substantial growth in routine bacteriology and antimicrobial susceptibility testing, strengthened reference and surveillance laboratory capacity, increased participation in external quality assessment, and expanded reporting to the World Health Organization's Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System. The program also supported complementary surveillance approaches, including antimicrobial use and consumption data and, in some settings, burden-of-disease and genomic surveillance. Progress, however, has been uneven and remains vulnerable to fragile infrastructure, procurement and supply chain bottlenecks, workforce turnover, fragmented data systems, weak clinical-laboratory interfaces, limited representativeness, and uncertain long-term financing. The Fleming Fund experience shows that strengthening AMR surveillance in LMICs is feasible, but requires sustained, system-wide investment. Future strategies should prioritize integration with clinical care, stronger digital and analytical capacity, broader diagnostic access, and domestic financing to ensure that high-quality AMR data are generated, shared, and translated into action.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance and One Health: Lessons on One Health Governance and Implementation from the Fleming Fund
abstract: This paper reflects upon the experience of the Fleming Fund in designing and implementing One Health antimicrobial resistance (AMR) programs in 25 countries and identifies practical lessons for the design of future One Health programs. The Fleming Fund experience highlights key priorities for implementing One Health effectively within AMR programs-though many of the insights should be applicable to other contexts as well, such as emerging infectious diseases and health security. One Health should be treated as an approach to problem framing and action rather than a program output, with flexibility for national adaptation. Meaningful implementation requires sustained investment beyond human health, particularly in animal and environmental sectors, to avoid symbolic engagement. Surveillance systems should consider both the role of the sector and sector-specific needs, supported by capacity for joint interpretation and use of evidence. The costs of multisectoral coordination should be explicitly resourced and both formal governance mechanisms and informal professional networks recognized as essential for building trust, sustaining collaboration, and translating data into policy-relevant action.

title: Surveillance Data Use Through the Fleming Fund: Informing Action on Antimicrobial Resistance in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
abstract: Drawing on the Fleming Fund's work to strengthen antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance across Africa and Asia during 2018-2026, this article provides one of the first syntheses of AMR surveillance data use in low- and middle-income countries. A participatory synthesis for narrative review was conducted to summarize experience across administrative levels (facility, subnational, national, and regional). Data use was most evident at the facility level, in human health systems where resistance patterns, antimicrobial use, and clinical data increasingly informed antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention and control, and other quality improvement initiatives. Data use in other sectors required different approaches. At the national level, Fleming Fund investments were associated with revisions of treatment guidelines, updates of essential medicines lists, and regulatory measures, primarily through improved governance and policy communities. Regional platforms supported member country data use at the national level. Subnational data use was undertaken in countries with decentralized health systems. Across levels, data use pathways driven by local priorities helped surveillance inform action. Fleming Fund experience suggests that surveillance is more likely to inform action when data use is built into system design. Continued investment will be needed if AMR surveillance is to improve policy and practice in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Surveillance: Ten Years On
Culture-based detection of clinically relevant carbapenemase genes in Gram-negative bacteria from aquatic environments in western Algeria
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) requires environmental surveillance because aquatic systems can receive resistant bacteria, antimicrobial residues and mobile resistance genes from domestic, agricultural, hospital and industrial sources. This culture-based study investigated culturable Gram-negative bacteria recovered from 12 inland, saline, wetland and coastal aquatic sites in western Algeria between January and April 2023. Bacterial isolates were identified by conventional biochemical methods and 16 S rRNA gene sequencing. Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed by disk diffusion and selected broth microdilution assays, with colistin interpreted only by minimum inhibitory concentration. Phenotypic screening for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-like and carbapenemase-associated activity was followed by targeted PCR and Sanger sequencing in selected high-risk isolates. Fifty-four Gram-negative isolates were recovered, including 44 fermenting and 10 non-fermenting isolates. Ten isolates, all fermenting Gram-negative bacteria, fulfilled the multidrug-resistant definition after exclusion of species-related intrinsic resistance. Targeted sequencing confirmed blaOXA-48 in two Escherichia coli isolates and one Cronobacter sakazakii isolate. One Escherichia coli isolate co-harbored blaNDM-1 and blaOXA-48. The colistin-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate was negative for mcr-1. These findings provide baseline evidence that selected aquatic environments in western Algeria harbor culturable Gram-negative bacteria carrying clinically important carbapenemase genes. The study should be interpreted as targeted culture-based surveillance rather than a quantitative assessment of the aquatic resistome. These data represent the environmental component of AMR surveillance within a One Health framework and do not establish an epidemiological linkage to human or animal reservoirs.

title: Alternative respiratory electron transport pathways drive differential aminoglycoside susceptibility
abstract: Bacterial bioenergetics is increasingly recognized as a central determinant of antibiotic tolerance and resistance. Here, we define how architectural variation within the aerobic electron transport system (ETS) modulates proton motive force (PMF) and governs antibiotic susceptibility. We constructed fourstrains with unbranched respiratory pathways differing in proton-translocation efficiencies. A low-PMF ETS variant exhibited selective tolerance to aminoglycosides, while susceptibility to β-lactams and tetracycline remained unchanged. Using fluorescent gentamicin, we demonstrate that reduced PMF directly limits drug uptake. Interestingly, wild-typewas as susceptible as the high-PMF variant. These results establish respiratory energy transduction as a mechanistic bottleneck for aminoglycoside efficacy and position ETS remodeling as a bioenergetic route to antibiotic tolerance.IMPORTANCEInfectious diseases remain a major global health challenge, and the failure of antibiotics to effectively treat them is compounding the threat. This study shows that the way bacteria produce energy can strongly influence how well certain antibiotics work. By engineering bacteria with different respiratory pathways, we demonstrate that bacteria in a low-energy state became specifically more tolerant to aminoglycoside antibiotics such as gentamicin and tobramycin. Importantly, this tolerance was linked to reduced drug entry into the cell rather than resistance gained due to acquisition of adaptive genetic change. The findings reveal that bacterial energy metabolism is not simply a housekeeping process, but a major factor determining antibiotic effectiveness. This work helps explain why some bacteria survive antibiotic treatment despite lacking resistance mutations and highlights bacterial respiration as a promising target for developing strategies to restore antibiotic sensitivity and combat persistent infections.

title: Protein malnutrition facilitates intestinal colonization with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae through disrupted intestinal microbial metabolism
abstract: Pediatric infections with highly resistant(HR-Kp) disproportionately affect low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Malnutrition is an identified risk factor for infection with HR-Kp and other antimicrobial-resistant Enterobacterales, but the mechanistic underpinnings of this link and independence from other common exposures, like antibiotics, in children are unclear. Using a murine model of pediatric malnutrition, we found that mice fed a protein-deficient diet (PD) were more susceptible to colonization with HR-Kp at a 4-log lower challenge inoculum and developed a 3-log higher intestinal burden in comparison to adequately nourished mice. HR-Kp colonization in PD-fed mice persisted beyond 5 weeks, and colonization was transmitted to diet-matched cage mates. Antibiotic treatment resulted in similar HR-Kp colonization burdens regardless of diet, suggesting that nutrition-dependent colonization risk is driven by altered intestinal microbiota. Despite reduced dietary protein intake, intestinal amino acid content was maintained in PD-fed mice, supporting optimal HR-Kp growth. Furthermore, secondary bile acids, prototypic intestinal microbiota-derived molecules, were reduced in PD-fed mice, demonstrated an inverse correlation with HR-Kp burden, and partially inhibited the growth of HR-Kp. Collectively, these findings reveal a role for dietary protein intake in determining nutrition-dependent colonization resistance to HR-Kp.IMPORTANCEAntimicrobial-resistantare responsible for a growing mortality burden worldwide, with disproportionate rates of infection in low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Several publications have demonstrated high rates of intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistantin children admitted with severe malnutrition in sub-Saharan Africa. However, numerous confounding risk factors in malnourished children (antibiotic use, healthcare exposure, and immune dysfunction) make it difficult to assess the direct impact of nutrition oncolonization. In this study, we utilized a novel mouse model of protein malnutrition to demonstrate that dietary protein deficiency renders mice susceptible to a higher burden of intestinal colonization at a lower inoculating dose of. Furthermore, reduced microbiota-derived bile acid metabolites correlate with increased burden of colonization in protein-deficient mice. These results are the first to establish a direct mechanistic link associating dietary protein deficiency, bile acid metabolism, and intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant.

title: Sequencing-based molecular epidemiology of mesophilic Aeromonas in dairy environments and water systems
