abstract: This study investigated the prevalence, virulence gene distribution, antimicrobial resistance, and molecular epidemiology of mesophilicspecies from milk, dairy farm environments, and drinking water systems in Kashmir, India.prevalence varied between sample sources, with environmental samples having the highest detection rate (51.96%), followed by water sources (46.60%) and milk (36.15%). Following pasteurization and disinfection, prevalence in milk samples was significantly reduced, demonstrating the efficacy of hygiene measures in minimizing contamination. Higher detection rates were found in environmental sources like soil, cow dung, and milkers' hands, suggesting their role as potential sources of contamination. The Aeromonads exhibited a wide distribution of virulence determinants; species-associated variations were noted for theandgenes, while thegene was ubiquitous among isolates. Virulence gene distribution differed between species, withexhibiting the most varied virulence profiles. Antimicrobial resistance patterns were generally comparable among the mesophilicspecies, and multidrug resistance was detected in 45.8% of the isolates. Analysis of,, andgenes based on sequencing distinguished isolates into species-specific clades, withproviding the highest intra-species resolution, suggesting its utility as an informative marker for molecular epidemiological investigations of. These results show that water systems and dairy environments are significant sources of genetically diverse Aeromonads carrying virulence and antimicrobial resistance determinants.IMPORTANCEspecies are widely distributed in aquatic environments and are increasingly recognized as emerging opportunistic pathogens, yet their role in dairy production systems remains poorly understood. The prevalence and genetic relatedness of mesophilicspp. across milk, dairy farm environments, and drinking water systems remain underexplored. By integrating prevalence data from a large and diverse collection of samples with virulence profiling, antimicrobial resistance characterization, and sequencing-based molecular epidemiology, the present study provides a comprehensive assessment ofpopulations across these interconnected compartments. The findings underscore the importance of hygienic practices during milk production and the need for routine monitoring of environmental and water sources associated with dairy systems. Improved understanding of the genetic diversity and distribution ofcan support more effective surveillance strategies and help mitigate potential risks to food safety and public health.

title: PASTA kinase dimerization in Enterococcus faecalis does not require the extracellular PASTA domains
abstract: The penicillin- and Ser/Thr-kinase-associated (PASTA) kinase family of bacterial signaling proteins encompasses a widely conserved family of transmembrane Ser/Thr kinases defined by the presence of multiple PASTA domains comprising the extracellular module. PASTA kinases are found in nearly all gram-positive bacteria and are activated in response to cell wall stress to control critical physiological processes. A thorough understanding of the mechanisms of PASTA kinase signaling is important not just for greater insight into bacterial physiology but also to target PASTA kinases for therapeutic intervention. However, many fundamental features of the proposed model for signaling by PASTA kinases have not been tested using full-length kinase in cells of its native host under physiological conditions; hence, the mechanisms of PASTA kinase signaling have remained largely obscure. In this work, we tested fundamental features of the proposed model for PASTA kinase signaling using the representative PASTA kinase of, IreK. Through a combination of genetics and biochemistry, we established that IreK participates in self-association to form dimers incells and that the self-associated form of IreK is functionally important for signaling. However, in contrast to the proposed model for PASTA kinase signaling, IreK dimerization does not require the extracellular PASTA module, and moreover, dimerization does not correlate with IreK signaling. Additionally, dimerization of IreK is not sufficient for kinase activation. Thus, regulation of PASTA kinase signalingis more complex than has been proposed.IMPORTANCEMost gram-positive bacteria encode penicillin- and Ser/Thr-kinase-associated (PASTA) kinases that are activated in response to cell wall stress to control critical physiological processes, including cell division and antibiotic resistance, among others. As such, PASTA kinases have been considered potential targets for new antibiotics. A thorough understanding of the mechanisms of PASTA kinase signaling is important for effective therapeutic intervention. However, the prevailing model for signaling by PASTA kinases has not been tested using a full-length kinase in cells of its native host under physiological conditions; hence, the mechanisms of signaling remain obscure. Here, we showed that the PASTA kinase ofparticipates in self-association to form dimers incells and that the self-associated form is functionally important for signaling. However, some features of the prevailing model for PASTA kinase signaling are inconsistent with our results, suggesting that regulation of PASTA kinase signalingis more complex than has been proposed.

title: The growing zoonotic threat of Babesia and Theileria: the urgent case for piroplasm-specific drug pipelines
NTDB: a curated database of natural transformation machinery and regulatory genes in prokaryotes
abstract: Natural transformation, genetically controlled by specialized machinery and regulatory genes, drives evolution and adaptation in prokaryotes. This process facilitates the spread of clinical traits such as antibiotic resistance. The DNA uptake specificity is mediated by conserved motifs found in certain naturally transformable species. Despite its evolutionary and clinical significance, dedicated resources for natural transformation have been lacking. Here, we present the Natural Transformation DataBase (NTDB) (https://bioinfo-mml.sjtu.edu.cn/NTDB/), which compiles information on machinery and regulatory genes associated with natural transformation in prokaryotes. NTDB integrated experimentally validated data on 118 naturally transformable species, 1072 transformation-associated genes, and 10 DNA uptake motifs identified through literature mining. Homology-based search identified 420 600 machinery genes and 246 164 regulatory genes across 12 310 prokaryotic strains, with comprehensive protein annotations. In addition, the distribution and abundance of DNA uptake motifs in Neisseriaceae and Pasteurellaceae species were quantified. Furthermore, NTDB offers online tools to predict natural transformation-associated genes and DNA uptake motifs via an interactive web interface. NTDB intends to facilitate mechanistic studies of natural transformation machinery and competence regulation.

title: Genomic diversity and antimicrobial resistance determinants among publicly available Mycoplasma genitalium genomes: a comparative phylogenomic analysis
abstract: BackgroundAntimicrobial resistance is increasingly challenging the clinical management ofinfections. This study aimed to characterize the genomic diversity, population structure, molecular typing profiles, and distribution of antimicrobial resistance-associated determinants among publicly availablegenomes.MethodsAll 64 genomes publicly available in NCBI and PubMLST at the time of data collection were included. Genomes were characterized byand MG309 molecular typing and screened for mutations associated with macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance. Phylogenetic relationships were investigated using a recombination-filtered core-genome alignment, and molecular typing and antimicrobial resistance profiles were mapped onto the resulting maximum-likelihood phylogeny.ResultsSubstantial molecular diversity was observed, with 29and 21 MG309 types identified. Macrolide resistance-associated 23S rRNA mutations were detected in 34/64 (53%) genomes. The fluoroquinolone resistance-associated ParC substitutions S83I and S83 R were detected in 14 (22%) and one genome, respectively. Relevant GyrA substitutions were less frequent and occurred exclusively in genomes also carrying ParC S83I. Overall, 15/64 (23%) genomes exhibited a dual-resistance genotype, whereas 19/64 (30%) carried macrolide resistance-associated mutations without concomitant fluoroquinolone resistance markers. Resistance-associated genotypes occurred across multiple phylogenetically distinct genomic backgrounds, while clusters of closely related isolates sharing molecular typing and resistance profiles were also identified. Conventionaland MG309 typing did not consistently recapitulate whole-genome phylogenetic relationships.ConclusionsThese findings reveal substantial genomic diversity and a high frequency of resistance-associated determinants among publicly availablegenomes, supporting the expansion of geographically representative genomic surveillance to monitor the emergence and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Production of recombinant human proteins in Komagataella phaffii using a sucrose-utilization-based selection marker without antibiotic resistance
abstract: Komagataella phaffii (K. phaffii) is one of the most widely used eukaryotic expression systems for recombinant protein production. However, its industrial application is constrained by reliance on traditional antibiotic-based selection and the inability to utilize sucrose. Based on the heterologous expression of the sucrose hydrolase SucF from Aspergillus flavus in K. phaffii, the strain acquired the ability to utilize sucrose. It was verified that this trait can serve as a dominant selection marker under sucrose-selective conditions, making SucF a selection marker for antibiotic-free strain construction. Under a selection pressure of 40 g/L sucrose, the gene integration efficiency reached 100 %, comparable to that of traditional antibiotic selection. Notably, this system enables the substitution of the original glycerol carbon source with sucrose for fermentation. To improve the selection efficiency of SucF, a triple mutant (T65A/R322Q/S323G) was identified through computer-aided protein engineering, exhibiting a 57 % increase in sucrose hydrolysis rate compared to the wild type. Structural analysis revealed that this mutation remodels the sucrose-binding pocket. Ultimately, the SucF mutant was used as a selection marker in combination with the histidine auxotrophic marker (HIS4) to achieve secretory expression of human lactoferrin (hLF) and human osteopontin (hOPN) in the GS115, and the resulting recombinant strain was free of antibiotic gene residues. This sucrose-based antibiotic-free platform in K. phaffii provides a promising strategy for green biomanufacturing and industrial production of recombinant proteins devoid of antibiotic resistance genes.

title: Global Distribution and Co-occurrence of Antimicrobial, Biocide, and Metal Resistance Genes in 11,921 Acinetobacter baumannii Genomes
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a critical priority pathogen globally. While antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) are well characterized, the prevalence, distribution, and co-occurrence patterns of biocide and metal resistance genes (BMRGs) remain poorly defined at global scale. We performed genomic analysis of 11,921 non-redundant A. baumannii genomes retrieved from NCBI RefSeq, representing isolates from 93 countries collected between 1982 and 2025. ARGs and BMRGs were identified using AMRFinderPlus (v4.2.7; organism-specific mode). Multilocus sequence typing (Pasteur MLST) was performed, and BMRG-ARG co-occurrence was assessed using one-sided Fisher's exact tests for enrichment with Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q < 0.05). Every genome carried at least one AMR determinant, and 99.98% carried at least one biocide or metal resistance locus at initial annotation. AMRFinderPlus identified 687 resistance-associated loci (633 AMR determinants; 39 biocide and metal resistance loci, of which 38 BMRGs were retained for analysis after exclusion of the core-genome gene nreB; and 15 virulence-associated loci, which were excluded from resistance analyses). Sequence type 2 (ST2) accounted for 56.4% of genomes. The carbapenemase gene blaOXA-23 was detected in 62.6% of genomes, and fluoroquinolone resistance mutations were highly prevalent (gyrA S81L: 84.9%; parC S84L: 77.2%). Co-occurrence analysis identified 38 significant BMRG-ARG associations overall (q < 0.05, OR ≥ 10), with a prominent module linking the integron-associated marker qacEΔ1 to ARGs (e.g., sul1, aadA1); the population-level mercury resistance-tet(A) association was not supported in the phylogeny-based sensitivity analysis. This study provides quantitative evidence for structured BMRG-ARG co-occurrence patterns in A. baumannii, shaped by ST2 dominance. These patterns are consistent with possible linkage and co-selection, although the present data cannot establish physical linkage.

title: Phage preferential infection of antibiotic-susceptible bacteria enriches antibiotic-resistant bacteria in activated sludge microbiomes
abstract: Despite the significance of phages in microbial ecosystems, the contribution of lytic phages to the propagation of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) within activated sludge microbiomes remains unclear. By integrating global metadata analysis and metagenomics, we first demonstrated that lytic phages exhibit a strong infection preference for antibiotic-susceptible bacteria (ASB, 70.84%) over antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB, 29.16%). This preferential phage infection was consistent with ARB carrying an exceptionally higher abundance of antiviral defense systems than ASB (averaging 1.83 versus 0.03 systems per whole genome). Furthermore, phage transplant experiments revealed that elevated phage predation pressure (phage-to-bacteria ratios ≥100) drove significant shifts in community composition toward highly defended lineages, thereby enriching the relative abundance of ARGs and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) by 25∼30-fold compared to controls. Additionally, real-time microfluidic tracking confirmed a "Kill-the-Winner" ecological dynamic, where phages selectively eradicate fast-growing ASB, thereby indirectly promoting ARB survival and increasing ARG transfer frequency. Overall, these findings highlight an underappreciated ecological risk driven by selective predation of lytic phages, which indirectly accelerates ARG dissemination in complex environmental microbiomes.

title: Acute Otitis Externa-Antimicrobial Resistance in the US and Canada: Phase III Study Outcomes
abstract: The goal of this investigation was to characterize the microbiological profile and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of pathogens isolated from AOE patients of 2 vehicle-controlled Phase III clinical trials and evaluate pathogen eradication rates achieved with finafloxacin otic suspension. In vitro MIC comparisons to other fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin) are reported as supplementary susceptibility data and do not reflect direct randomized clinical comparisons. A total of 2683 bacteria isolated from 1234 AOE patients enrolled in 2 Phase III clinical studies in the United States, Puerto Rico, and Canada were analyzed. Specimens were collected from the external ear of subjects with AOE. Species-level identification for each bacterial isolate recovered was obtained by combining phenotypic and genotypic data. End point minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing was performed using Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute recommended methods. 72.7% of the pre-therapy bacteria were Gram-positive and 27.3% Gram-negative. Most frequent bacterial isolates werespp. (46.7%) followed byspp. (19.5%). Methicillin resistance was detected in 17.0% of.(MRSA) and 33.2% of.(MRSE) isolates. Ciprofloxacin resistance was identified in 12.5% of.and 14.0% of.isolates. Finafloxacin eradicated 86.4% of the MRSA isolates and 80.6% of the MRSE isolates. Finafloxacin eradicated ciprofloxacin-resistantspp. in 74.4% and ciprofloxacin-resistantspp. in 87.5% of treated patients. Finafloxacin demonstrated high eradication rates in AOE patients with methicillin-resistant.and., as well as in patients with ciprofloxacin-resistantspp.- andspp., irrespective of the pathogen's resistance profile. These in vitro findings, together with observed eradication rates in the vehicle-controlled trials, suggest that finafloxacin may offer advantages in the treatment of resistant organisms, particularly under acidic pH conditions. However, direct clinical trial comparisons have not been conducted. Clinical trial registry name: ClinicalTrials.gov. URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/. Identifier: NCT01535599 and NCT01535560.

title: Eco-friendly biosynthesis of silver nanoparticles by saprophytic Fusarium solani as a sustainable therapeutic approach for the management of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus wound infections
abstract: The rising prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has prompted the exploration of novel, naturally sourced therapeutic alternatives. Here, the saprophytic fungus Fusarium solani was used to biosynthesize silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), which were characterized by UV-visible spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The AgNPs showed a surface plasmon resonance peak at ~ 410 nm, a zeta potential of - 42.7 mV, an average TEM diameter of 19.58 nm, and a hydrodynamic (DLS) diameter of 121.4 nm with a polydispersity index of 0.302. Against clinical methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) isolates, the AgNPs exhibited minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) values of 0.1875-0.375 mM, with confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) showing a reduction in bacterial viability from 92.3% to 28.0% and TEM revealing marked ultrastructural membrane damage following treatment. In a murine MRSA wound infection model, AgNPs treatment increased wound healing from 12.33% to 95.33% and reduced bacterial load from 9.90 to 1.10 log CFU/g tissue relative to the untreated infected control, alongside significant downregulation of TNF-α, IL-6, and COX-2 expression and improved histopathological indices of tissue repair (all p < 0.05). These findings indicate that fungal-derived AgNPs possess potent antibacterial and wound-healing properties against MRSA, supporting their potential as a sustainable therapeutic candidate, although further mechanistic and translational studies are needed.

title: Repeat antimicrobial susceptibility testing of serial bacterial isolates: clinical utility and diagnostic stewardship
abstract: To synthesize evidence on the interpretation and temporal stability of antimicrobial susceptibility profiles in serial bacterial isolates and to identify factors that inform repeat testing within diagnostic stewardship. This narrative review integrates evidence from studies of serial clinical isolates with data on analytical variability, within-host resistance evolution, heteroresistance, antimicrobial exposure, and diagnostic stewardship. Susceptibility profiles are generally stable over short intervals, although clinically relevant changes vary according to bacterial species, antimicrobial agent, specimen context, and elapsed time. Small MIC shifts, particularly near clinical breakpoints, may result in categorical discordance without indicating true resistance emergence. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exhibits greater short-term phenotypic variability than several other common pathogens. Repeat AST is most strongly supported when infection persists or recurs, the clinical response is inadequate, antimicrobial exposure may have selected for resistance, or the consequences of missed resistance are substantial. In selected lower-risk settings, referral to a recent susceptibility result may be appropriate, provided that laboratory and clinical override mechanisms remain available. Short-term susceptibility stability may support conservative referral to a recent AST result, but the degree of instability varies by organism, antimicrobial agent, and specimen context. Where a single operational interval is required, laboratories may adopt the shortest interval supported by local or otherwise applicable evidence, with predefined overrides for higher-risk clinical situations. Prospective multicentre validation is required before specific intervals can be generalized across clinical and laboratory settings.

title: Quorum sensing and quenching as integrated strategies for antimicrobial resistance mitigation in aquaculture: Applications and future directions
abstract: The rapid expansion of aquaculture has been accompanied by an increased prevalence of bacterial diseases, leading to widespread antibiotic use and the accelerated emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Rising water temperatures and environmental stressors further exacerbate pathogen proliferation and disease outbreaks, posing significant threats to global aquaculture productivity and sustainability. Quorum sensing (QS), a bacterial cell-to-cell communication system, plays a central role in regulating virulence factor expression, biofilm formation, and AMR-related pathways in aquatic pathogens. Consequently, disrupting QS through quorum quenching (QQ) has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional antibiotic-based treatments. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the mechanisms underlying QS and its role in AMR development in aquaculture systems. It highlights various QQ strategies, including enzymatic degradation of signaling molecules, competitive inhibition using small-molecule quorum sensing inhibitors, and the application of probiotic organisms capable of interfering with QS pathways. Evidence from recent studies demonstrates that QQ can effectively reduce virulence, enhance antibiotic sensitivity, and lower the required dosage of antimicrobial agents. Despite its potential, the implementation of QQ in aquaculture faces several challenges, including environmental stability, scalability, species-specific variability in QS systems, and regulatory concerns. Future research should focus on developing broad-spectrum, non-toxic, and environmentally stable QQ agents, as well as improving delivery systems for practical field applications. Overall, quorum quenching represents a promising, eco-friendly strategy to mitigate AMR, reduce antibiotic dependence, and enhance the sustainability of aquaculture systems worldwide.

title: Biofilm-mediated pathogenesis in staphylococcal bovine mastitis: A mechanistic review of virulence, pharmacokinetic barriers, and advanced anti-biofilm therapeutic strategies
abstract: Bovine mastitis remains one of the most economically significant infectious diseases affecting dairy production worldwide, causing substantial losses through reduced milk yield, treatment costs, and premature culling. Among the causative agents, Staphylococcus aureus and non-aureus staphylococci (NAS) are particularly problematic due to their capacity to establish chronic intramammary infections through biofilm formation, facilitating immune evasion and marked antimicrobial tolerance. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review integrates mechanistic and translational evidence on biofilm-mediated pathogenesis, pharmacokinetic barriers, and anti-biofilm interventions in staphylococcal bovine mastitis. A structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection was conducted for investigations published between January 2015 and February 2026. From 513 identified records, 26 primary empirical studies met all eligibility criteria and were synthesized. Mechanistically, staphylococcal biofilm development entails initial adhesion mediated by microbial surface components recognizing adhesive matrix molecules (MSCRAMMs), followed by extracellular matrix accumulation governed by the icaADBC operon responsible for polysaccharide intercellular adhesin (PIA/PNAG) synthesis, alongside ica-independent pathways orchestrated by the biofilm-associated protein (Bap) and extracellular DNA (eDNA). These developmental stages and dispersal dynamics are coordinated by the agr quorum-sensing system and the global regulator sarA. Comparative genomic evidence indicates that NAS species, particularly Staphylococcus chromogenes and Staphylococcus haemolyticus, harbor specialized virulence and antimicrobial resistance determinants that drive subclinical persistence. Beyond bacterial determinants, antimicrobial efficacy is severely constrained by mammary pharmacokinetic barriers, including non-specific drug binding to milk proteins, sequestration in fat globules, and rapid clearance during milking cycles. Emerging therapeutic strategies notably phytochemical-loaded nanoemulsions, matrix-dispersing enzymes, and bacteriophage endolysins-demonstrate substantial capacity to dismantle established biofilms and restore antimicrobial susceptibility in preclinical models. Overcoming persistent staphylococcal mastitis will require translating dual-action formulations combining matrix-degrading agents with advanced delivery systems into validated intramammary therapeutics.

title: Engineering Vibrio natriegens for biopesticide production: from pathway optimization to plant protection
abstract: Phytopathogens pose a persistent threat to global crop production, necessitating the development of sustainable biocontrol strategies. Microbial biopesticides offer a promising alternative to chemical pesticides; however, their industrial application is frequently constrained by low production titers and high substrate costs. This study reprograms the phenazine-1-carboxylic acid (PCA) biosynthetic pathway in Vibrio natriegens, a fast-growing marine bacterium with broad carbon utilization capability. A modular plasmid toolbox is constructed through systematic optimization of promoters, ribosome binding sites, replication origins, and antibiotic resistance markers, enabling high-level PCA production. To address plasmid instability and antibiotic dependence, an I-SceI-based genome editing platform is established, facilitating scarless, multi-copy chromosomal integration of the PCA gene cluster. The final engineered strain, Vna6, achieves PCA titers of 102.0 mg/L in shake flasks and 579.8 mg/L in fed-batch fermentation with glucose as the carbon source. Furthermore, Vna6 exhibits broad-spectrum antagonistic activity against both bacterial (Streptomyces scabies) and fungal (Glomerella cingulata) phytopathogens, as confirmed by in vitro inhibition zone assays and in vivo plant protection experiments on Arabidopsis thaliana and radish seedlings. This work establishes V. natriegens as a potenial chassis for biopesticide production and offers a promising strategy for sustainable crop disease management.

title: Bats, wild rodents, and marsupials as ecosentinels of antimicrobial resistance: a systematized narrative review of resistance genes, mobile genetic elements, and One Health implications
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major One Health challenge, yet wildlife remains underrepresented in surveillance systems. This systematized narrative review synthesized studies published between 2011 and 2025 on antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in bats, wild rodents, and marsupials, aiming to evaluate their role as reservoirs, disseminators, and ecosentinels of environmental AMR. The search was conducted in PubMed, SciELO, MEDLINE, and Scopus, and original studies reporting bacterial identification and phenotypic or genotypic resistance data were included. A total of 110 studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising rodents (n = 56), bats (n = 37), and marsupials (n = 17). The most frequently reported bacterial groups included Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus spp., Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterococcus spp., and Salmonella spp. Rodents frequently harbored multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales, including ESBL-producing E. coli and resistance genes associated with last-line antimicrobials, reflecting exposure to urban, agricultural, and waste-contaminated environments. Bats were prominent reservoirs of resistant Staphylococcus spp., including methicillin-resistant strains, and carried clinically relevant Gram-negative bacteria, likely influenced by mobility, diet, colony behavior, and anthropogenic landscape exposure. Marsupials generally showed lower AMR burdens in free-ranging conditions, but captive and rehabilitated individuals exhibited increased resistance, suggesting human-mediated acquisition and amplification. Across host groups, the detection of mobile genetic elements and resistance determinants shared with clinical contexts supports the occurrence of cross-ecosystem exchange. These findings reinforce the need to integrate wildlife into AMR monitoring frameworks as early-warning indicators of environmental contamination and resistance dissemination.

title: Microalgae-based removal and biodegradation of antibiotics: mechanisms, synergistic consortia, and engineering prospects
abstract: Antibiotic pollution in aquatic environments drives the spread of resistance genes and threatens ecosystem health. Microalgae offer a dual-function platform that both senses antibiotic stress and actively removes these contaminants. This review synthesizes current knowledge on microalgae-based antibiotic removal and biotransformation, emphasizing the integration of biosorption, enzyme-mediated transformation-primarily via cytochrome P450 and nitroreductase-and co‑metabolic processes. We highlight the phycosphere as a dynamic interface where symbiotic bacteria enhance algal survival and pollutant removal, while also modulating the enrichment and dissemination of resistance genes. Algal-bacterial granular sludge systems illustrate the practical potential of this synergy, achieving efficient antibiotic removal and suppression of resistance propagation. Emerging tools such as immobilization, synthetic biology, and machine learning show potential to further improve system robustness and may facilitate precision process control, although their scalability and long-term performance remain to be validated. By linking fundamental mechanisms with engineering strategies, this review provides a framework for developing sustainable, low-carbon bioremediation technologies aligned with global antimicrobial resistance action plans.

title: Genomic and functional characterisation of exopolysaccharide biosynthesis in marine bacterium Alteromonas sp. PRIM-28 with emulsifying and anti-inflammatory activities
abstract: Bacterial exopolysaccharides (EPS) are structurally heterogeneous biopolymers governed by species- and strain-specific biosynthetic pathways and with diverse biotechnological applications. The study investigated EPS biosynthesis in a marine bacterium, Alteromonas sp. PRIM-28 through an integrated genomic and experimental approach. Whole-genome sequencing and functional annotation were performed to identify the gene clusters and regulatory elements associated with EPS biosynthesis. The salt tolerance of the bacterium was studied at salt concentrations of up to 25%. EPS production was assessed using the ethanol precipitation method and partial characterisation, including emulsification and anti-inflammatory assays. Draft genome contained 3444 coding sequences with 97.6% completeness. Phylogenetic and ANI analyses confirmed its close relation to Alteromonas fortis (96.2%). Genome mining identified wzy-dependent and generic-cellulose EPS biosynthesis clusters along with the presence of epsCDEFHLM genes. CAZyme and KEGG analysis revealed diverse carbohydrate-active enzymes and complete central carbohydrate metabolism pathways, supporting EPS biosynthesis in PRIM-28. Presence of saline and oxidative stress-tolerance genes (nqrABCDEF, opuED, sglTSBC and katABEG) suggest bacterium's environmental adaptability. Genes associated with virulence factors and antimicrobial resistance were not identified supporting the suitability of the strain for industrial use. The strain tolerated salinity up to 15%. The highest EPS production was seen at 96 h (2.40 ± 0.09 g L). The EPS contained ~ 60% total sugars, showed emulsification activity against different oils, and exhibited anti-inflammatory activity in the albumin denaturation assay (80.7 ± 0.9%) comparable to positive control (p > 0.05). The combined genomic and functional evidence establishes the EPS biosynthesis in PRIM-28 and highlight its potential as a sustainable biopolymer source.

title: Genomic Characterization of Multidrug-Resistant Enterobacter hormaechei from Bovine Raw Milk: Implications for Food Safety and Public Health
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in foodborne bacteria poses a growing threat to public health. In this study, multidrug-resistant Enterobacter hormaechei (E. hormaechei), a member of the Enterobacter cloacae complex (ECC), was isolated from bovine raw milk in Gujarat, India, and examined for its prevalence, antimicrobial resistance, and genomic characteristics. A total of 21 presumptive E. hormaechei isolates were recovered from 190 raw milk samples (11.05%) based on morphological and biochemical characteristics and further confirmed using a species-specific PCR assay. Based on their phenotypic antimicrobial resistance profiles, eight multidrug-resistant (MDR) isolates were selected for whole-genome sequencing and downstream genomic analyses. Whole-genome sequencing of the MDR isolates revealed distinct sequence types, with ST350 and ST68 clustered closely. The sequenced isolates harbored a diverse repertoire of antimicrobial resistance genes, including blaACT, qnrS1/qnrB7, fosA, oqxA/B, mph(A), and aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, consistent with their multidrug-resistant phenotypes. Virulence profiling identified genes associated with iron acquisition, adhesion, stress response, and type VI secretion systems, suggesting the presence of virulence-associated genetic determinants. Plasmid replicons (IncFII and Col-type) and the insertion sequence IS26 were identified among the sequenced isolates. This study provides a genomic characterization of MDR E. hormaechei isolates from raw milk in Gujarat, India, and emphasizes the importance of continuous AMR surveillance to monitor the spread of Enterobacter lineages with relevance to food safety and public health.

title: From Spore Biology to System Performance: Strain-Resolved Mechanisms, Biosafety and Translational Readiness of Bacillus Probiotics in Aquaculture
abstract: Bacillus-based probiotics are widely promoted as antibiotic-sparing interventions in aquaculture, yet translation from controlled trials to commercial production remains constrained by strain heterogeneity, inconsistent dosing, incomplete biosafety assessment and frequent inference of mechanisms from non-specific biomarkers. This scoping review reorganizes the evidence reported for 67 empirical studies published during 2015-2025 into a strain-host-route-system framework. Across finfish and aquatic invertebrates, Bacillus supplementation was commonly associated with improved growth, feed utilization, digestive-enzyme activity, mucosal or systemic innate immune indices, challenge survival and, in water-applied or biofloc settings, nitrogenous-waste control. The evidence nevertheless does not support a universal optimal dose: reported regimens span colony-forming units per gram or kilogram of feed, colony-forming units per millilitre of culture water and mass-based commercial formulations, and efficacy varies with strain identity, host developmental stage, delivery route, diet, salinity, temperature and challenge design. Mechanistic support is strongest for pathogen antagonism, enzyme provision, barrier modulation and environmental bioremediation, whereas claims concerning stable colonization, antiviral action and antimicrobial-resistance mitigation are often indirect. Bacillus should therefore be evaluated at strain rather than genus level, with whole-genome screening for virulence determinants, toxins, transferable resistance genes and mobile elements. We propose a translational-readiness framework integrating identity, potency, formulation stability, host compatibility, environmental persistence, biosafety and farm-scale validation. This reframing positions Bacillus probiotics as promising but conditional tools for antibiotic stewardship and One Health-aligned aquaculture.

title: Lipid Extract from Ulva ohnoi Algae: Chemical Characterization, Antibacterial Potential, and Cytotoxicity in the Search for New Agents Against MDR Infections
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a critical global concern. This study explored the lipid extract (LE) of Ulva ohnoi regarding its chemical composition, antibacterial activity, and cytotoxicity against multidrug-resistant (MDR) microorganisms. The LE was characterized by GC-MS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Antibacterial efficacy was determined by Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) and Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC) against MDR isolates: Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and coagulase-negative Staphylococci (CoNS). Cytotoxicity was evaluated in murine fibroblast (L929) and bovine renal fibroblast (MDBK) cells using MTT, Neutral Red (NR), Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH), and hemolytic activity (HA) assays. Lipid characterization revealed palmitic acid (63.62%) and oleic acid (21.01%) as major components. TGA indicated 88% mass loss, and DSC showed no amorphous/crystalline domains. LE showed favorable MIC values against S. aureus and CoNS (1.33 mg/mL) and against A. baumannii and E. coli (2 mg/mL), indicating moderate antibacterial activity typical of an unfractionated crude extract. MBC results indicated bacteriostatic activity (1-8 mg/mL). The extract was cytotoxic to L929 and MDBK cells at concentrations close to its MIC (IC₅₀ 0.25-1.95 mg/mL) but well tolerated by blood cells (HA IC4.705 mg/mL). U. ohnoi LE extends, rather than establishes, the previously reported antibacterial potential of Ulva lipids through comprehensive chemical characterization and MDR-isolate evaluation. However, low selectivity indices (SI < 10) indicate that the LE does not yet present an adequate therapeutic window, reinforcing the need for bioassay-guided purification. Nevertheless, it is a starting point for developing new antibacterial agents.

title: Combined antibacterial and antibiofilm activity of an Ag-CeO₂/MgAl-LDH nanocomposite-nanoemulsion formulation against multidrug-resistant Enterococcus faecium
abstract: The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) Enterococcus faecium has created an urgent need for alternative antimicrobial strategies capable of overcoming conventional antibiotic resistance and inhibiting biofilm formation. In the present study, the antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of an Ag-CeO₂/MgAl-LDH nanocomposite, a sunflower oil-based nanoemulsion, and their combined formulation were evaluated against both a clinical MDR isolate and the reference strain E. faecium MCC 2763. The prepared formulations were characterized using dynamic light scattering (DLS), zeta potential analysis, and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. Antibacterial activity was assessed by minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC), time-kill kinetics, impedance-based growth monitoring, bacterial adherence assays, and biofilm inhibition studies. The combined nanocomposite-nanoemulsion formulation showed greater antibacterial and antibiofilm activity than the individual formulations under the experimental conditions evaluated. Time-kill and biofilm assays indicated improved inhibition of bacterial growth and biofilm formation, while impedance measurements further supported the antibacterial activity of the combined formulation. Although the present findings demonstrate the promising antibacterial potential of the developed formulation, formal synergy analysis, cytotoxicity evaluation, advanced physicochemical characterization, and mechanistic investigations were beyond the scope of this study. These investigations will be essential in future work to further evaluate the therapeutic potential of this formulation. Overall, the developed Ag-CeO₂/MgAl-LDH nanocomposite-nanoemulsion formulation represents a promising antibacterial platform for combating multidrug-resistant Enterococcus faecium and warrants further investigation through comprehensive preclinical evaluation.

title: Addressing threats to future global health-what is the right timeframe?
Identification of atypical Escherichia coli as hidden reservoir of tet(X4)-positive IncX1 plasmid
abstract: The horizontal dissemination of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) poses a significant threat to public health. In this study, we investigated the presence and transferability of a tet(X4)-positive IncX1 plasmid in an atypical Escherichia coli isolate, GX-3-49. Genomic analysis revealed that GX-3-49 is markedly distinct from conventional E. coli, characterized by a reduced gene repertoire, fewer toxin genes, and a distinct phylogenetic lineage. Phenotypic characterization further demonstrated that, compared to the reference strain EC25922, GX-3-49 exhibits diminished motility, growth, and virulence, alongside a marked increase in biofilm formation and pH tolerance, but greater sensitivity to high temperature. These findings suggested that GX-3-49 might have evolved a fitness trade-off, reducing its virulence in exchange for enhanced resilience under acidic and biofilm-forming conditions. Additionally, a tet(X4)-positive IncX1 plasmid co-harboring bla, tet(A), and floR, was identified in GX-3-49 and remained stable during serial passaging. This plasmid exhibited high sequence similarity to IncX1 plasmids previously identified in E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae and was capable of conjugative transfer to E. coli EC600, suggesting its potential for interspecies dissemination. In conclusion, this study identified a stable and transferable tet(X4)-positive IncX1 plasmid in an atypical E. coli strain exhibiting reduced virulence and increased susceptibility to heat, yet enhanced stress resilience under specific environmental conditions. These findings highlight the potential of such bacteria to serve as hidden reservoirs for antimicrobial resistance and facilitate the dissemination of ARGs.

title: Molecular epidemiology of NDM-producing Enterobacterales in Huai'an, China: Genomic diversity and evaluation of aztreonam-avibactam and cefiderocol
abstract: Metallo-β-lactamase-producing carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (MBL-CRE) pose a serious threat due to antimicrobial resistance. However, their prevalence in the Huai'an region of Jiangsu Province in eastern China remains unknown. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) isolates collected from Xuyi People's Hospital were screened for carbapenemase production using the modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM) and EDTA-modified carbapenem inactivation method (eCIM), followed by PCR confirmation. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing, biofilm formation assays, growth kinetics analyses, and whole-genome sequencing with bioinformatics were performed to characterize the isolates. The 12 NDM-producing Enterobacterales identified comprised seven Escherichia coli, three Klebsiella pneumoniae, and two Enterobacter hormaechei. Beyond carbapenem resistance, resistance to aztreonam, tetracycline, fluoroquinolones, and aminoglycosides was common among the isolates. Four isolates (including three E. coli) showed intermediate susceptibility to cefiderocol, and the aztreonam-avibactam combination exhibited synergistic activity against aztreonam-resistant Enterobacteriaceae isolates. Genomic analysis revealed eight isolates carrying bla, three carrying bla, and one carrying bla. All isolates belonged to distinct sequence types, including two novel types. The NDM-13 isolate and one NDM-1-positive E. hormaechei isolate displayed distinct genetic contexts, whereas most isolates harbored a bla-ble-trpF-tat-dct genetic structure. Among the three cefiderocol-intermediate E. coli isolates, mutations were identified in cirA and ftsI. This study reveals the prevalence and diverse genetic backgrounds of MBL-CRE in Xuyi County, demonstrates the potent activity of aztreonam-avibactam, and suggests that cefiderocol resistance may involve multiple factors.

title: Facilitating non-radical peroxymonosulfate oxidation of tetracyclines driven by struvite crystallization
abstract: Eliminating residual antibiotics during struvite recovery from livestock wastewater is essential to prevent the spread of antibiotic resistance. In this work, the effects of in-situ struvite crystallization on the degradation of typical veterinary antibiotics, tetracyclines (TCs), by non-radical peroxymonosulfate (PMS) oxidation were investigated. Results revealed that the process of struvite crystallization enhanced PMS oxidation of TCs with kvalues reaching 1.95-2.15 times those of PMS alone.Oand electron transfer processes were identified as the dominant non-radical pathways. Electrochemical analyses indicated that electron transfer processes would be more active through crystallization than pre-formed crystals in PMS oxidation due to the higher interfacial reactivity. Mg:P molar ratio and pH affected TCs degradation through regulating struvite crystallization and altering the speciation of TCs and PMS, with Mg:P ratio of 1.0 and pH 9.2-9.8 being optimal for facilitatingOgeneration and PMS oxidation. In the presence of humic acid (HA), HA-TCs complexes caused an inhibitory effect on TCs degradation, and excess Mgmitigated this inhibition by reducing the direct association between TCs and HA. Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS) and fluorescence spectroscopy analyses revealed that HA underwent selective molecular restructuring, with nitrogen-containing and highly condensed aromatic components being converted into more oxygenated and less aromatic products through oxygenation, which could further favor electron transfer pathways. This study highlights that struvite crystallization enhances non-radical oxidation and provides new insights into antibiotic removal with simultaneous phosphorus recovery in livestock wastewater.

title: Salmonellosis outbreaks associated with pork, United States, 2012-2021
abstract: Nontyphoidal Salmonella causes an estimated 1.3 million domestically-acquired foodborne infections in humans annually in the United States (Scallan Walter et al., 2025). From 1998 to 2023, pork was the fourth most common food category attributed to foodborne Salmonella illnesses (Interagency Food Safety Analytics Collaboration, 2024). We analyzed salmonellosis outbreaks associated with pork products between 2012-2021, using data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Foodborne Diseases Outbreak Surveillance System, System for Enteric Disease Response, Investigation, and Coordination, PulseNet, and the National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System. There were 50 Salmonella outbreaks linked to pork from 2012-2021. Twenty-one different Salmonella serotypes were identified; serotype I 4,[5],12:i:- was the most common, causing 19/50 outbreaks, followed by Typhimurium (7/50). Raw ground pork was associated with three outbreaks (6%) and 444 illnesses (23%). Pork roast or shoulder was associated with 13 outbreaks (26%) and 408 illnesses (21%). Whole pigs were associated with 11 outbreaks (22%) and 368 illnesses (19%). Among Salmonella isolates with available antimicrobial resistance information, 226/389 (58%) showed multidrug resistance and 230/389 (59%) showed clinically significant resistance; 216/222 (97%) and 22/34 (65%) of I 4,[5],12:i:- and Typhimurium isolates, respectively, exhibited any resistance. Antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella isolates from outbreaks linked to pork was more frequent than for nontyphoidal Salmonella infections in the United States overall. Preharvest disease prevention efforts that target serotypes I 4,[5],12:i:- and Typhimurium may be valuable in reducing Salmonella outbreaks and illnesses. Downstream exploration of individual- and community-level factors related to handling, preparation, and consumption of specific pork types may help reduce salmonellosis rates through targeted education.

title: Global phylogenomic structure and accessory resistance dynamics of Acinetobacter baumannii ST2
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii sequence type 2 (Pasteur ST2), associated with international clone 2, is a major antimicrobial-resistant lineage, but its within-lineage population structure and accessory resistance variation remain incompletely resolved. We analyzed 5612 quality-filtered public genomes from an existing global dataset using PopPUNK, core-genome SNP analysis, AMRFinderPlus, MobileElementFinder and MOB-suite. A dominant PopPUNK cluster contained 5604 genomes (99.86%). Its SNP phylogeny showed dense short-distance relationships within a connected lineage; pairwise distances had a median of 314 SNPs. Four antibiotic classes-beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, phenicols and fosfomycin-were detected in at least 95% of dominant-cluster genomes. The median antibiotic-class annotation hit count was 14 per genome (IQR, 13-15), including intrinsic and lineage-associated determinants. Predicted conjugative and mobilizable plasmid signatures occurred in 52.6% and 42.7% of dominant-cluster genomes, respectively. Across the full cohort, mobile-element and antibiotic-class hit counts were weakly positively correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.191). This unadjusted association was absent among 700 representatives selected one per ≤10-SNP component (ρ = -0.0721; p = 0.0567), and a component-bootstrap interval included zero. Assembly-adjusted associations differed between the full cohort and representatives. The small positive unadjusted collection-year association was not robust to location adjustment and was unsupported in dated representatives. Complete-genome annotations documented both chromosomal and plasmid blacopies and upstream ISAba1 proximity, without establishing promoter activity or resistance phenotype. These findings describe a cohesive ST2 lineage with heterogeneous accessory resistance and plasmid-mobility signatures, while emphasizing the sensitivity of genome-wide associations to assembly characteristics and clonal and geographic sampling.

title: When is travel-health AI inference transportable? Mobility-conditioned admissibility for cross-border disease risk and decision support
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used for infectious disease surveillance, traveller risk assessment, outbreak forecasting and decision support. Travel creates a distinctive transportability problem because people move between epidemiological, geographic, climatic and healthcare contexts in which the conditions supporting an inference may change rapidly. This conceptual/theoretical methodological-development study was informed by a targeted narrative review of travel medicine, infectious disease surveillance, human mobility, border health, mass gatherings, antimicrobial resistance and health-AI validation literature. We develop a mobility-conditioned admissibility framework that treats travel as movement across origin, transit, destination and return regimes. Interpretation is conditioned on mobility state, epidemiological regime, exposure history, time-dependent constraints and clinical or biological constraints. Five proposed operational states are retained: supported inference, conditionally transportable inference, active monitoring, restricted interpretation and withholding. The framework also distinguishes low probability from infeasibility and requires preservation of rare but epidemiologically feasible events. Model availability and conventional predictive validity do not establish inferential transportability across changing travel contexts. Mobility-conditioned admissibility provides a complementary use-boundary layer for travel health AI by making cross-regime support explicit before outputs are interpreted or released. Its incremental value requires prospective evaluation against calibrated uncertainty, external validation and dataset-shift monitoring.

title: Conjugative IncHI1 plasmids drive the emergence of multidrug resistance in Nigerian Salmonella Typhi: A four-decade genomic analysis
abstract: The role of plasmids in driving antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in West African Salmonella Typhi remains unexplored. This study investigates the prevalence, temporal dynamics, and genetic associations of plasmid mobility classes and replicon types in Nigerian S. typhi over nearly four decades. We analyzed 151 S. typhi genomes from Nigeria (1982-2018) obtained from EnteroBase. Plasmid replicon typing and mobility classification revealed that 49.7% of isolates harbored conjugative plasmids, with the IncHI1 family (IncHI1A, IncHI1B_R27, and IncFIA_HI1) being the most prevalent. Conjugative plasmids increased from 0% in the 1980s to 56% in the 2010s (logistic regression, p = 0.006). A core multidrug resistance element comprising blaTEM-1B, sul1, catA1, dfrA15, and tet(B) was identified in 49% of isolates. Strong statistical associations were observed between IncHI1 plasmids and these AMR genes, with phi coefficients reaching r = 0.95 for tet(B), r = 0.87 for blaTEM-1B, and r = 0.86 for sul1. Isolates carrying conjugative plasmids harbored nearly five times more AMR genes than non-mobilizable isolates (4.9 vs 0.9; ANOVA, p < 0.001). Temporal breakpoint analysis identified 2010 as the year AMR prevalence exceeded 50%, coinciding with the sharp rise in conjugative plasmid carriage. Conjugative IncHI1 plasmids are the primary drivers of multidrug resistance emergence in Nigerian S. typhi, carrying a conserved core resistome that has spread rapidly since 2010. These findings underscore the critical need for plasmid surveillance in genomic epidemiology and highlight IncHI1 plasmids as key targets for monitoring AMR transmission in high-burden settings.

title: Prevalence, management, and outcomes of urinary tract infections in older adults living in care homes versus older adults living outside care homes in the UK: a propensity score-matched case-control analysis
abstract: Globally, rising drug-resistant urinary tract infections (UTIs) affect older populations disproportionally. We aimed to assess the incidence, management, and patient outcomes of UTIs in English care homes. Using linked primary, secondary, social care, and pathology data covering 2·5 million patients in London between 2018 and 2023, we matched older adults with UTIs living in care homes with older adults living outside care homes using propensity scores. We performed a time-series analysis of incidence and compared urine culture turnaround time and results (including antimicrobial resistance). We assessed UTI-related patient outcomes, including death, complications, recurrent infection, and antibiotic re-prescription within 60 days, using generalised estimating equations, adjusted for demographic and other risk factors. We identified 91 501 UTI cases, including 6648 (7·3%) in care homes. In care homes, 4678 (70·4%) of the 6448 UTIs occurred in women and 3779 (56·8%) involved individuals aged 85 years or older. The older adults living in care homes were older (median age: 86 years [IQR 80-91] vs 76 years [71-83]) and more frequently White (70·3% vs 56·7%) than older adults living outside care homes. The incidence rate of community-acquired UTIs was 1909·4 per 100 000 person-months in care homes (increasing by 3·7 [95% CI 0·8-6·6] per month), as compared with 543·5 outside care homes (decreasing by 1·3 [-1·8 to -0·7] per month). Urine cultures were used less (1366 [20·5%] of 6648 [95% CI 19·6-21·5] vs 24 699 [29·1%] of 84 853 [28·8-29·4]), were more likely to be polymicrobial (suggesting contamination; 416 [30·4%] of 1366 [28·1-32·9] vs 4325 [17·5%] of 24 699 [17·0-18·0]), and had a longer turnaround time (52·9% turnaround in 1 day [50·3-55·6] vs 66·2% [65·6-66·8]) in care homes than outside care homes. Escherichia coli UTIs had higher resistance to trimethoprim (46·4% [95% CI 41·0-51·9] vs 32·0% [30·9-33·1]) and nitrofurantoin (7·5% [4·9-10·8] vs 2·4% [2·0-2·8]) in care homes than outside care homes. Care home cases had significantly worse 60-day outcomes, with higher risk of death (1·99 [95% CI 1·67-2·36]; p<0·001), presenting to general practitioners (1·38 [1·01-1·89]; p=0·042) and to hospitals (1·15 [1·01-1·32]; p=0·041) with complications, recurrent infections (1·22 [1·08-1·36]; p=0·001), and antibiotic re-prescription (1·11 [1·01-1·21]; p=0·024). Older adults residing in care homes had higher UTI infection burden and worse clinical outcomes than matched older adults residing outside care homes. Possible explanatory factors include inadequate care, discordant prescribing decisions, and disconnect with diagnostic capabilities, in addition to the exacerbating effects on infection management during the COVID-19 pandemic. These findings highlight the need for improvement in infection management in care home settings. National Institute for Health and Care Research; Wellcome Trust; Fleming Initiative.

title: Corrigendum to "International implementation of ASIARS-net for AMR surveillance: Building on JANIS" [Journal of Global Antimicrobial Resistance 50 (2026) 236-245]
Water-Soluble Chlorophyll Proteins as Biocompatible Photosensitizers for Photodynamic Therapy to Combat Antibiotic Resistance and Biofilm Through Disrupting Bacterial Membranes
abstract: The escalating crisis of antibiotic resistance and biofilm-associated infections urgently demands therapeutic strategies with distinct mechanisms of action. Antibacterial photodynamic therapy (abPDT) offers a promising alternative, yet its clinical translation is often limited by the poor solubility, low biocompatibility, or complex delivery requirements of conventional photosensitizers (PSs). Here, we report the application of recombinant water-soluble chlorophyll proteins (WSCPs) from the Brassicaceae family as fully natural, self-contained PSs for abPDT. WSCP forms exceptionally stable tetrameric complexes with chlorophylls, providing outstanding water solubility, high photostability, negligible dark toxicity, and food-grade biocompatibility. Upon 660 nm light irradiation, WSCP-mediated abPDT achieves broad-spectrum killing of clinically relevant Gram-positive (including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, MRSA) and Gram-negative bacteria and effectively disrupts mature biofilms. Mechanistically, WSCP adheres to bacterial surfaces and generates singlet oxygen in situ, causing rapid membrane permeabilization, leakage of intracellular contents, and cell death, through a resistance-evading, physical mode of action. In a murine MRSA-infected wound model, a single topical application of WSCP followed by light exposure significantly reduces bacterial burden, suppresses inflammation, accelerates tissue regeneration, and promotes wound closure without observable toxicity. This work establishes WSCP-based abPDT as a safe, simple, and highly effective platform to combat antibiotic-resistant and biofilm-associated infections.

title: Occurrence, spatial distribution, and ecological and human health risks of antibiotic residues in the River Jhelum
abstract: Antibiotic residues in riverine environments are emerging contaminants of concern because of their persistence, ecological effects, and potential contribution to antimicrobial resistance. This study investigated the occurrence, spatial distribution, pollution status, and screening-level ecological and human-health risks of six antibiotics in the River Jhelum, Pakistan. Surface-water samples were collected from ten monitoring sites representing upstream, midstream, and downstream reaches during a post-monsoon sampling campaign. Antibiotics were quantified using High Performance Liquid Chromatography coupled with photodiode-array detection, while single-factor and comprehensive pollution indices and GIS-based spatial interpolation were applied to characterize contamination patterns. Azithromycin exhibited the highest concentration (20.30 µg/L), followed by ofloxacin (12.70 µg/L), ciprofloxacin (8.03 µg/L), linezolid (4.55 µg/L), cefixime (1.40 µg/L), and levofloxacin (0.51 µg/L). Azithromycin showed the greatest pollution burden across the monitoring sites investigated, whereas levofloxacin exhibited comparatively limited contamination. The comprehensive pollution assessment indicated substantial combined antibiotic contamination across the investigated river transect. Azithromycin produced the highest ecological risk quotient (RQ = 17.41), indicating high predicted ecological risk under the applied screening framework. Human health hazard quotients remained below unity, indicating non carcinogenic risks. These findings strengthen wastewater management, pharmaceutical discharge controls, and systematic monitoring of antibiotic residues in the River Jhelum.

title: Carbonic Anhydrases in Mycobacteria: Linking Metabolic Adaptation to Phenotypic Drug Tolerance
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) treatment is increasingly challenged by both antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and phenotypic drug tolerance, the latter representing a reversible physiological state that contributes to persistence and prolonged therapy. While AMR is driven by heritable genetic mutations, drug tolerance arises from reversible physiological adaptations that enable bacterial survival during prolonged antibiotic exposure. Increasing evidence suggests that metabolic remodeling plays a central role in establishing these drug-tolerant states. Carbonic anhydrases (CAs) are zinc-containing metalloenzymes that catalyze the reversible interconversion of carbon dioxide and bicarbonate, thereby maintaining intracellular pH homeostasis and supporting bicarbonate-dependent metabolism. Beyond their established metabolic functions, indirect evidence suggests that CAs may contribute to physiological adaptations associated with bacterial persistence under host-imposed stresses, including hypoxia, nutrient limitation, and acidic environments. Although they are not classical AMR determinants, CAs may influence the metabolic landscape associated with phenotypic drug tolerance. In this review, we examine current evidence supporting the role of CAs in mycobacterial metabolism and propose a conceptual framework linking bicarbonate homeostasis, intracellular pH regulation, and metabolic adaptation to bacterial persistence and drug tolerance. We further discuss the potential of carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs) as adjunctive agents whose ability to enhance the activity of conventional antitubercular drugs requires experimental validation, together with the value of experimental models, including the Mycobacterium marinum-zebrafish system, and computational approaches for validating CA-targeted therapeutic strategies. Overall, this review highlights CAs as candidate metabolic regulators that may influence the physiological state underlying phenotypic drug tolerance. Defining their mechanistic contribution to persistence could facilitate the development of metabolism-based therapeutic strategies that complement existing TB treatment.

title: Optimization, characterization, and mechanistic evaluation of iturin and surfactin like, broad spectrum antimicrobial lipopeptides from Bacillus subtilis RKEA1 isolated from Acanthus ilicifolius
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) continues to rise globally, largely due to limited discovery of novel antimicrobial agents capable of overcoming resistance mechanisms associated with conventional antibiotics. This challenge underscores the need to explore alternative bioactive compounds. In the present study, an endophytic Bacillus subtilis strain, RKEA1, isolated from Acanthus ilicifolius collected from an area near the Kadalundi wetland mangrove forest (Kerala, India), was evaluated for its antimicrobial potential. The culture supernatant had broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive bacteria such as S. aureus, S. pyogenes, C. violatium and L. monocytogenes, and Gram-negative bacteria including K. pneumoniae, E. coli, P. aeruginosa, Shigella spp., Proteus mirabilis, S. enterica and Y. enterocolitica, and also the fungi C. albicans and C. neoformans. Bioactive lipopeptides were extracted and subjected to comprehensive characterization, including determination of molecular weight, Rf value, and mass profiling. Production parameters were optimized, and physicochemical stability of the lipopeptides were examined under varying environmental conditions. Response surface methodology (RSM) based medium optimization enhanced lipopeptide production by 1.8-fold. The minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of the lipopeptides were 31 µg/mL against the tested Gram-positive bacteria and 62.5 µg/mL against Gram-negative bacteria. The minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) against Gram-positive bacteria was 62.5 µg/mL. Furthermore, mechanistic investigations provided insight into the mode of action, revealing membrane disruptive activity. Importantly, this work offers a detailed characterization of antimicrobial lipopeptides from the endophytic Bacillus subtilis RKEA1 isolated from Acanthus ilicifolius by optimizing lipopeptide production, physicochemical stability studies, antimicrobial activity and membrane-disruptive activity. Overall, the findings highlight Bacillus subtilis RKEA1 as a promising source of antimicrobial lipopeptides with potential applications in combating resistant bacterial infections and contributing to the development of novel therapeutic agents.

title: Climate-extreme soil exposome: how drought converts contaminated agricultural soils into one-health risk hotspots
abstract: Contaminated agricultural soils are conventionally treated as static pollutant repositories whose hazard state is adequately captured by total contaminant concentration, an assumption that intensifying drought regimes are rendering untenable. This review advances the concept of a climate-sensitive soil exposome, in which drought functions as a hydro-biogeochemical driver that reorganizes the bioavailability, speciation, and biological accessibility of metals, antibiotics, pesticides, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, and microplastics without altering their total soil inventories. By reducing porewater connectivity, concentrating solutes within disconnected microsites, and expanding the air-water interfacial area, drought can modify the spatial co-localization and interactions among pollutant classes whose mixture-level exposure potential cannot be predicted from single-contaminant assessments. At the same time, drought imposes ecological filtering on soil microbial communities, selectively enriching stress-tolerant, biofilm-forming, and resistance-bearing taxa that, in soils co-contaminated with persistent metals and antibiotic residues, disproportionately expand antibiotic resistance genes and mobile genetic elements. Global evidence now associates aridity with elevated hospital-level antibiotic resistance rates (i.e., the frequency of resistant clinical isolates recorded in hospital surveillance data) across 116 countries, implicating climate-driven soil microbial filtering in public health consequences extending far beyond field boundaries. Drying-rewetting cycles emerge as periods of potentially elevated exposure, generating acute pulses of contaminants, resistant microorganisms, and resistance genes through crop uptake, contaminated dust inhalation, and post-drought hydrological export pathways that static, concentration-anchored monitoring frameworks may not fully capture. Future risk assessment should consider drought-rewetting transitions as primary sampling targets, adopt bioavailability-resolved and mixture-sensitive monitoring, and explicitly incorporate contaminated agricultural dust as a critically undercharacterized inhalation exposure route, prioritizing it as a research frontier in climate-sensitive soil exposome science.

title: Whole-genome sequencing and antibiotic resistance analysis of a clinical carbapenem-resistant Enterobacter chuandaensis
abstract: This study aimed to characterize a rare clinical isolate,, carrying the carbapenem resistance gene. The antimicrobial susceptibility analysis revealed thatEC001 was resistant to the majority of commonly used antimicrobial agents, except for amikacin, chloramphenicol, and minocycline. The results of the modified carbapenem inactivation method and EDTA-modified carbapenem inactivation method confirmed thatEC001 produces metallo-β-lactamase.EC001 was typed as sequence type 2493 and presented an extensive drug-resistant profile. Whole-genome sequencing analysis demonstrated that the strain harbors two plasmids (p1_EC001 and p2_EC001), among whichis located on the conjugative plasmid p1_EC001 of IncFIB/IncFII-type. Plasmid p1_EC001 could be transferred into, indicating its interbacterial horizontal transmission potential. The majority of plasmid-mediated resistance genes reside within or adjacent to various mobile genetic elements in p1_EC001. In addition, an3000 element (3,018 bp) was detected upstream of, while the bleomycin resistance-related genewas located downstream of, followed by,,,,, andKpn19. Moreover, one class 1 integron harboring the genetic arraywas identified on p1_EC001. The plasmid p2_EC001 was characterized as a mobilizable plasmid, and two key genes,and, were detected, which encode the plasmid mobilization relaxase MbeA and the accessory protein MbeC, respectively. In summary, this study demonstrated the antimicrobial susceptibility, plasmid features, and potential transmission mechanisms ofEC001, which serve as evidence for controlling and prevention of clinical.IMPORTANCECurrent research on carbapenem resistance inremains relatively limited. This study performed detailed genome characterization of the two plasmids (p1_EC001 and p2_EC001) carried byEC001 and analyzed their resistance gene profiles, plasmid features, and potential transmission mechanisms. The findings provide a theoretical foundation for the formulation of hospital infection control strategies, improve the capability for early warning and prevention of carbapenem-resistant, and exhibit substantial scientific significance, as well as promise clinical application value.

title: Antibiotic Stewardship, Resistance, and Mortality in Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococcus: A Quasi-Experimental Study of Linezolid Restrictions
abstract: Antibiotic restriction policies are intended to curb resistance, but their effects on resistance, timely treatment, and patient outcomes remain uncertain. We evaluated linezolid restrictions and whether vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) screening identifies patients most likely to benefit. We conducted a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences study using electronic health record data from 521,493 admissions at 2 academic medical centers from 2008 through 2019. Hospital 1 introduced a formal prior-authorization pager system in 2011 and stricter linezolid-specific criteria with enhanced post-prescription review in 2014; Hospital 2 served as a control. Outcomes included linezolid use, linezolid-resistant Enterococcus isolates, in-hospital mortality overall and by VRE status, and stewardship request behavior. Linezolid was used in 2.3% of admissions; 1.2% of Enterococcus isolates were linezolid resistant. Restriction policies were associated with a 27% reduction in linezolid use (-0.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -1.1 to -0.7; P < .001) and a 41% reduction in resistance (-1.0 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -1.6 to -0.4; P = .003). Overall mortality did not increase, but mortality among VRE-screen-positive patients increased by 4.7 percentage points (95% confidence interval, 1.9 to 7.5; P < .001), with larger increases among those with bacteremia or sepsis. Approval rates declined first, followed by fewer linezolid requests. Restriction policies can reduce antibiotic use and resistance but may benefit from screening-informed safeguards to preserve timely treatment for high-risk patients.

title: Integrative multi-omics reveals CUL4B as a modulator of macrophage pyroptosis and innate defense against Staphylococcus aureus
Research on the spillover risk of antibiotic resistance gene from the gut microbiome of wild animal: A case study of the golden snub-nosed monkey
abstract: Wild animals are "reservoirs" of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), and the interface of rivers between wild animals and humans is an ideal environment for spreading ARGs. In order to explore the risk of ARGs from wild animals to the human ecosystem through rivers, metagenomic sequencing was used to obtain the microbiome in the gut of golden snub-nosed monkeys () and in the rivers. We performed collinearity analysis between the high-risk ARGs (Rank I ARGs) from golden snub-nosed monkeys and the metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from river samples to assess the potential of river microorganisms to acquire Rank I ARGs. The number of collinear events between Rank I ARGs and MAGs in the WHD group (rivers within the disturbed monkey habitat) was five times higher than that in the WCK (rivers within the undisturbed monkey habitat) group. This implies a significant spillover risk of ARGs from wild animals to the human ecosystem via river interfaces, a risk that is further intensified by human disturbances. This research complemented the content that evaluated the spillover risk of ARGs from wild animals to humans.

title: Network-based characterization of latent co-testing patterns in antimicrobial susceptibility testing
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance depends on antimicrobial susceptibility testing, yet antibiotic panels vary by pathogen cohort, specimen, year, ward, and care setting. We term these empirically reconstructed testing architectures shadow antibiograms: structures that shape which susceptibility results enter surveillance datasets and which resistance relationships can be observed. We analyzed approximately 13 million bacterial isolates from Germany's National Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance system (2019-2023) across six WHO BPPL-aligned operational cohorts. Co-testing networks were constructed using Jaccard, Dice, cosine, and phi-coefficient similarity, evaluated with Fisher's exact tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and partitioned with multi-resolution Louvain community detection. Networks contained three to four dominant co-testing communities; false discovery rate (FDR) retention ranged from 89 to 100% across cohorts and specimen types. Jaccard provided the best balance of coherence, stability, antimicrobial-class alignment, interpretability, and edge retention. This work provides one of the first national-scale empirical characterizations of shadow antibiogram structure, supporting diagnostic stewardship and bias-aware AMR surveillance interpretation.

title: Bionic nanocoating-mediated near-infrared persistent luminescence photodynamic system for the treatment of periprosthetic joint infection
abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a catastrophic complication of arthroplasty, notoriously difficult to treat due to bacterial biofilms and escalating antibiotic resistance. To address this, we designed a smart, biomimetic photodynamic coating (PL-PS@Ti) for titanium implants, utilizing near-infrared persistent luminescence nanoparticles (NLPLNPs) to achieve deep-tissue, on-demand antibacterial and osteogenic efficacy. We synthesized chromium/europium-doped zinc gallate NLPLNPs coated with dendritic mesoporous silica and conjugated with a silicon phthalocyanine photosensitizer (ZGO NP@DMSN-Si-Pc, or PL-PS). A copper-coordinated polyphenol network anchored these nanocomposites to titanium substrates. We evaluated the acid-responsive singlet oxygen (O₂) generation and 808 nm-reactivable afterglow of the coating, followed by validation in cell cultures and a rat PJI model. The acidic PJI microenvironment triggered robustO₂ generation, which was sustained by periodic 808 nm excitation. In vitro, the coating was highly biocompatible and achieved a 99.5% bactericidal rate. In the rat PJI model, 808 nm activation effectively cleared periprosthetic bacteria and resolved local inflammation. The coating also promoted osseointegration, yielding a bone volume fraction (BV/TV) of 20.66% at the implant interface four weeks post-treatment. The PL-PS@Ti nanocoating provides a microenvironment-responsive, antibiotic-free strategy to manage implant infections. By utilizing reactivable persistent luminescence, it bypasses the thermal damage risks of continuous irradiation. This dual capacity for broad-spectrum bactericidal activity and bone regeneration offers a practical and translatable intervention for arthroplasty-associated infections.

title: Epidemiologic determinants of antimicrobial resistance in feline urinary Escherichia coli in the United States (2018-2024)
abstract: Lower urinary tract infections are less common in cats than in dogs, with Escherichia coli being the predominant bacterial pathogen responsible for these infections. Although antimicrobial therapy is used for optimal treatment, repeated or prolonged exposure may increase the risk of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This study examined risk factors for AMR in urinary E. coli isolates from cats across the United States, focusing on prior positive cultures and other host, socioeconomic, and geographic factors, using multilevel logistic regression models, accounting for clustering at the patient, county, and state levels. From 2018 to 2024, antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) was performed on 138,695 clinical urinary E. coli isolates from 122,048 cats. The log-odds of antimicrobial non-susceptibility (ANS) increased linearly with the number of positive cultures in the preceding six months. After adjustment, isolates from cats in non-metropolitan counties had higher odds of non-susceptibility for most antimicrobials, compared with those from metropolitan counties. Every 1% rise in the annual county-level percentage of cats with positive culture and AST was associated with a 1-3% lower odds of ANS (p < 0.001). Additionally, isolates from cats in states with 1500-1999 housing units per veterinarian had higher odds of non-susceptibility across all antimicrobialscompared with those in states with 500-999 housing units per veterinarian, except fluoroquinolones. Patient-level factors, particularly recent repeated positive cultures, play a dominant role in AMR in feline urinary E. coli, likely reflecting the cumulative impact of long-standing resistant infections or antimicrobial exposure. Other findings may reflect differences in access to veterinary care or diagnostic testing, or differences in test submission patterns.

title: Biomaterials for environmental control of AMR dissemination
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens human, animal, agricultural, and environmental health, driven by horizontal and vertical gene transfer.
