Conventional wastewater treatment removes 63-94% of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) but fails to eliminate ARGs and antibiotic-resistant bacteria, while generating toxic sludge. This review evaluates advanced biomaterials, including silver and gold nanoparticles, reactive oxygen species, magnetic nanocomposites, targeted disruption of metabolic pathways, carbon-based sorbents, biopolymers, metal-organic frameworks, functionalized enzymes/peptides, and engineered biofilms, for reducing ARG and resistant-bacteria loads, inhibiting horizontal gene transfer, and reducing the selective pressure exerted by residual antibiotics. These approaches offer enhanced performance across wastewater/agriculture/air/food supply chain systems. Challenges in scalability, ecological safety, and regulation remain, requiring integration with AI monitoring, CRISPR tools, and One Health strategies. This review aims to summarize and discuss the literature on the development and use of innovative biomaterial-based intervention strategies that address the environmental aspects of AMR in order to provide a comprehensive overview of what has been learned and developed to date.

title: A Retrospective Benchmark of Quantitative Antimicrobial Peptide Activity Prediction Tools
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are critical candidates for addressing the global antibiotic resistance crisis. AI-driven quantitative models capable of directly predicting peptide antimicrobial activity, specifically minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), are gaining scientific prominence by providing precise guidance for the rational design of AMPs. To assess their real-world, out-of-the-box performance, we conducted a retrospective benchmark of 10 publicly released quantitative AMP prediction tools spanning classical machine learning and contemporary deep learning approaches. Using an external dataset and reconstructed native datasets, we evaluated absolute MIC regression, retrospective reproducibility, directional prediction patterns, ranking capability, and virtual-screening enrichment. Most released tools exhibited poor absolute MIC regression and limited transferability to the external benchmark, while selected tools retained useful relative-ranking and enrichment capabilities. Retrospective evaluation further revealed marked differences in implementation-level reproducibility among the released tools. Error-stratified analyses identified systematic associations between prediction errors and peptide residue composition, together with a general compression of the predicted activity range. Collectively, these findings characterize the practical performance boundaries of currently accessible quantitative AMP prediction tools and support their use primarily as early-stage screening filters rather than precise substitutes for experimental MIC measurements.

title: Spatial Variation of Antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli along Bagmati River, Kathmandu Valley
abstract: Antimicrobial resistant Escherichia coli has been reported in Bagmati river of Kathmandu Valley; however, studies on its spatial distribution are lacking, despite being essential for effective water management. Therefore, this cross-sectional study was conducted to determine the spatial distribution of antibiotic-resistant E. coli along Bagmati river from March-September 2025. This work was conducted at Department of Microbiology Tri-Chandra Multiple Campus. Water samples collected in duplicate from fifteen sites of Bagmati river were processed for most probable number count and isolation of E.coli. BOD and DO were calculated by Winkler's titrimetric method. Antibiotic susceptibility test was done by disk diffusion technique. Chi square test, correlation assessment, cluster and factor analysis were conducted. The coliform count, E. coli isolates, Biochemical oxygen demand and dissolved oxygen levels ranged from 5-26,500 MPN/100 mL, 0-42, 1.2-418.75 mg/L, and 8.05-0.15 mg/L, respectively, from Baghdwar to Chobar. No E. coli isolates were recovered from Site 1. Cluster analysis based on these variables classified river into four distinct segments, with Sites 1 and 15 forming separate clusters. Significant differences were observed in antibiotic resistance pattern of E. coli isolates across the sampling sites. Factor analysis further grouped the river sites into five clusters, indicating spatial variation in antimicrobial resistant E. coli along the river continuum. Conventional water quality indicators are insufficient to capture spatial complexity of river health. Integrating fecal contamination and antibiotic resistance patterns provides a more comprehensive assessment of pollution hotspots, supporting targeted management strategies under Nepal's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0.

title: Priorities and opportunities for strengthening hygiene and One Health alignment in research, policy and practice
abstract: Hygiene plays a critical yet under-recognized role in addressing One Health (OH) challenges, including zoonotic disease prevention, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) control, food safety and protection of ecosystem health. Likewise, hygiene research and interventionsgenerally lack an OH perspective, resulting in siloed efforts that inadequately address the human-animal-environment interface. We convened three sessions at global conferences well attended by health professionals working in hygiene or OH. Participants identified gaps and opportunities for hygiene-OH alignment across research, policy and practice at community, national, regional and global levels. An evidence gap identified was research on hygiene approaches to protect ecosystems in programs otherwise focused upon human or animal health. Methodological priorities included harmonizing tools and protocols for pathogen detection, fecal contamination measurement and hygiene behavior assessment; strengthening cross-sectoral data sharing; and developing integrated study designs. Intervention opportunities included engaging local stakeholders, balancing infrastructure and behavior change, adapting existing programs for cross-sectoral relevance and broadening evaluation to include animal and environmental outcomes. Implementation priorities included localized program design and decision-making, regional cooperation for cross-border threats and leveraging surveillance and preparedness infrastructure. Policy priorities included reducing institutional fragmentation, harmonizing standards, and strengthening the roles of hygiene and OH within existing regulatory frameworks. From our synthesis, we present cross-cutting recommendations for strengthening hygiene and OH alignment. Aligning hygiene and OH offers a pathway to more comprehensive and upstream prevention of disease and AMR, supporting coordinated, system-level management of health risks across human, animal and environmental domains and building resilience to emerging health threats.

title: Emergence of ESBL-Producing Escherichia coli in Shrimp Aquaculture, Kerala, India
abstract: The present study evaluated 63 shrimp aquaculture farm sites in the Thrissur and Alappuzha districts of Kerala State, India. A total of 206 samples were analyzed, and 50 extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli strains were identified with antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) profiles. All the strains were multidrug-resistant (MDR), with multiple antibiotic resistance (MAR) indices ranging from 0.32 to 0.64. PCR detection revealed a high prevalence of ESBL genes, bla(86%), bla(58%), bla(50%), DHA (58%) and bla(48%). Quinolone and fluoroquinolone genes are aac(6')-Ib-cr (100%), qnrS (78%), OqxA (52%), OqxB (18%) and qnrB (8%). Non-ESBL genes included tetA+tetB (98%, 2%), sul1+sul2 (90%, 76%) and cmlA (48%). Plasmid replicon typing showed that IncFIB and IncN (96%), IncI1 (92%), IncFIC (78%) and IncFIA (56%) as predominant plasmid types. Phylogrouping revealed the presence of pathogenic lineages B2 (40%) and D (14%), whereas phylogroups E (86%) and C (82%) were more prevalent. Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) demonstrated high genetic heterogeneity among the strains, indicating non-clonal dissemination across farms. These findings indicate a surge in ESBL-producing E. coli exhibiting elevated resistance mechanisms, posing a significant public health threat. This underscores the urgent need for coordinated cross-sectoral interventions to mitigate AMR risks, curb the dissemination of resistance genes, and safeguard aquatic ecosystems and public health.

title: When does environmental antimicrobial resistance become a health risk?
abstract: Environmental antimicrobial resistance (AMR) only constitutes a meaningful risk when resistant bacteria overcome key ecological and transmission barriers to reach, persist in, and colonize susceptible hosts. By linking exposure, evolution, transmission, and ecology, our framework provides a realistic basis for assessing AMR risks across One Health compartments.

title: Antimicrobial resistance trends and lineage distribution among invasive pneumococcal disease isolates pre- and post-pneumococcal conjugate vaccine introduction, South Africa
abstract: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV) have reduced antimicrobial-resistant invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) globally. We evaluated trends in antimicrobial-resistant IPD and pneumococcal lineages before and after PCV13 introduction in South Africa. We analysed national, laboratory-based IPD surveillance reported cases (2005-2020) and compared the incidence of resistant-IPD pre- and post-PCV introduction. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed for six antibiotics, and penicillin-multidrug resistance (penicillin-MDR) was defined as penicillin nonsusceptibility plus resistance to ≥2 additional antibiotic classes. Whole-genome sequencing was used to determine serotypes, sequence types, global pneumococcal sequence clusters (GPSC), and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants. Following PCV introduction, overall IPD and AMR IPD incidence declined substantially. Penicillin-cotrimoxazole nonsusceptible and penicillin-MDR IPD incidence decreased from 5.6 to 0.8 per 100,000 population (percentage decrease -86.5%, confidence intervals [CI] -90.5% to -81.4%) and 5.5 to 0.4 (-93.0%, -95.7% to -89.1%), respectively, in children <5 years, with smaller but significant reductions in the ≥5 years old. Despite these declines, residual PCV13 serotypes, particularly 19A and 19F, continued to contribute notably to penicillin-cotrimoxazole nonsusceptible and penicillin-MDR IPD, respectively, after PCV13 introduction. Non-vaccine serotypes (10A, 15A, 15B/C, 16F, 23B, and 35B) increasingly contributed to resistant IPD in the post-PCV13 era through the expansion of both vaccine-type and non-vaccine-type GPSC lineages. PCVs substantially reduced AMR IPD in South Africa, but persistent PCV13 serotypes and expanding resistant non-vaccine-type lineages highlight the potential benefit of higher-valency PCVs, including PCV20.

title: Eleven-year surveillance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections and antimicrobial resistance trends in a Portuguese tertiary hospital, 2014 - 2024: Trends and insights into novel agents
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a frequent hospital-associated pathogen, often causing severe infections with limited treatment options due to increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains. This study evaluated its prevalence and resistance patterns in a large tertiary hospital. A retrospective observational study analysed all P. aeruginosa clinical isolates collected over 11 years (2014-2024) from inpatients and outpatients. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing included carbapenems, cephalosporins, piperacillin-tazobactam, aztreonam, aminoglycosides, ciprofloxacin, fosfomycin, colistin, ceftolozane-tazobactam and ceftazidime-avibactam. A total of 22883 P. aeruginosa isolates were analysed, representing 16802 episodes from 9978 patients. Mean patient age was 60.9 ±24.7 years, with male predominance. The prevalence of P. aeruginosa among hospitalized patients was 3.0%. Overall, 11.9% of isolates were MDR, 3.3% XDR and 84.8% non-MDR, with MDR and XDR rates increasing over time (p<0.05). A difficult-to-treat phenotype was present in 4.2%. Resistance to at least one carbapenem was observed in 19.0% of isolates, and to ciprofloxacin in 20.3%. Susceptibility to piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, ceftazidime, and amikacin remained above 80%. Most isolates non-susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftazidime remained susceptible to amikacin, supporting amikacin-containing combination regimens in high-risk settings. Colistin resistance remained below 1%. Among MDR isolates, susceptibility to ceftazidime-avibactam decreased between 2017 and 2024 (100.0% to 83.7%, p<0.05), whereas ceftolozane-tazobactam susceptibility fluctuated over time (83.1% to 88.2%, p<0.05). These findings reveal a shifting resistance landscape and underscore the need for sustained surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, and updated empirical treatment strategies, while highlighting a critical gap in contemporary epidemiological data.

title: High prevalence of hypervirulent Staphylococcus aureus CC22-t309 in Pediatric Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis in China
abstract: This study aimed to elucidate the molecular epidemiology, virulence factors, and antimicrobial resistance profiles of Staphylococcus aureus isolated from children with osteomyelitis and septic arthritis (OM-SA) in China. A total of 68 S. aureus isolates were collected from pediatric patients with OM-SA in Shanghai, China, with 100 strains from children with other infections serving as controls. We performed a systematic analysis on all strains by integrating clinical metadata, whole-genome sequencing, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Among S. aureus isolates from OM-SA cases, CC22-t309 was the dominant clone (32.3%), followed by CC59-t437 (17.6%). The prevalence of CC22-t309 in OM-SA was much higher than that in the control (32.3% vs. 8.0%, p<0.001). OM-SA patients with CC22-t309 infection presented much higher inflammatory markers than those infected with other clones (p<0.05). Notably, CC22-t309 from OM-SA exhibited higher carriage of virulence factors, including Panton-Valentine leukocidin (pvl, 100%), collagen adhesin (cna, 86.4%), and fibronectin-binding proteins (fnbA/B, 77.3%), compared with other clones (pvl, 0∼66.7%; cna, 0∼13.8%; fnbA/B, 0∼24.1%; p < 0.05). Within CC22-t309 clone, the carriage of pvl, fnbB and fnbA showed no difference between OM-SA and control group (pvl: 100% vs. 87.5%; fnbB: 77.3% vs. 85.7%; fnbA: 77.3% vs. 37.5%; p >0.05). However, the prevalence of cna in OM-SA was significantly higher than that in the control group (86.4% vs. 37.5%, p = 0.015). Furthermore, CC22-t309 isolates displayed a multidrug-resistant phenotype against β-lactams, macrolides, and lincosamides. We identify the hypervirulent and multidrug-resistant CC22-t309 as a high-risk S. aureus lineage associated with pediatric OM-SA.

title: Implementation of rapid pan-microbial metagenomics in paediatric intensive care: a single-centre, prospective, observational study
abstract: Few clinical metagenomics studies have reported rapid results with associated clinical impact or described deployment of protocols beyond centres in which they were developed. We aimed to assess the feasibility and clinical impact of implementing a previously validated rapid pan-microbial respiratory metagenomic service in paediatric intensive care, reporting protocol modifications, feasibility, diagnostic performance, clinical impact, and staff perspectives. This single-centre, prospective, observational study was carried out at a general paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) and a cardiac paediatric ICU in Great Ormond Street Hospital (London, UK) between Nov 4, 2024, and Feb 28, 2025. Respiratory samples were obtained from patients selected by intensive care staff based on clinical suspicion of lower respiratory tract infection, with no exclusion criteria. Samples were analysed by a well-established published metagenomic workflow that simultaneously detects bacteria, fungi, and DNA and RNA viruses and provides same-day preliminary results and next-day final results; separate aliquots were sent for concurrent culture and PCR testing. Clinical impact (change in antimicrobials, diagnosis, or infection control) was evaluated through electronic health record review. Clinical staff were surveyed for their feedback via an anonymous online semistructured questionnaire. 177 samples from 122 patients (median age 3·4 months [IQR 1·2-36·0]; 54% male) were tested. 174 (98%) samples passed quality control. Sensitivity at 16-h sequencing was 89% (95% CI 80-95) for bacteria, 100% (70-100) for fungi, and 87% (76-93) for viruses, with specificities greater than or equal to 99% across all kingdoms. 42 (24%) of 174 samples analysed by metagenomics yielded 50 organisms that were not detected by routine diagnostics, all of which were confirmed by orthogonal PCR testing. Clinical impact was observed in 51 (29%) of 174 samples, comprising changes in antimicrobial therapy in 46 (26%) samples. Of these 46 samples, 15 (33%) resulted in cessation of antibiotics, ten (22%) in initiation of antibiotics, six (13%) in a change of antibiotic therapy, and 15 (33%) provided confidence to continue an empirical antibiotic choice. Of the 33 ICU staff members surveyed, 23 (72%) reported a positive view of metagenomics, none reported negative views, and 22 (67%) perceived additional benefits over routine testing. This clinical pilot of rapid respiratory metagenomics in paediatric intensive care showed high specificity and good sensitivity. Protocols developed for an adult population were adapted to a paediatric population, including adaptations for polymicrobial upper respiratory tract samples, which are more common in children. However, increased sensitivity and antimicrobial resistance prediction will be required for broader clinical implementation. Although changes in patient management were observed, particularly for antimicrobial stewardship, delineating the true contribution of metagenomic results offered by this study is difficult. Multicentre studies over multiple winter seasons, with control arms and predefined selection of patients and sample types, are needed to assess the impact on patient outcomes and cost-effectiveness. NHS Respiratory Metagenomics Network (NHS England).

title: Antimicrobial Resistance and Molecular Epidemiology of Enterococcus Species Isolated at the University Hospitals of Sfax, Tunisia
abstract: Enterococci are major causes of both community-acquired and healthcare-associated infections. The rapid global dissemination of multidrug-resistant clones poses a major challenge to clinical management and infection control. The aim for the present study was to investigate the prevalence, antimicrobial resistance patterns, virulence genes, and molecular epidemiology of Enterococcus species isolated from clinical specimens in university hospitals of Sfax, Tunisia. A descriptive, hospital-based, cross-sectional surveillance study was conducted between March 2020 and February 2021. It included all Enterococcus strains isolated in the Microbiology Department of Habib Bourguiba University Hospital. Enterococcus isolates were tested for antimicrobial susceptibility in accordance with European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing guidelines. Polymerase chain reaction assays were performed to detect resistance genes (vanA, vanB, ermA, ermB, ermC, msrA, mefE, vga, vat, vgb), virulence genes (gelatinase [gelE], aggregation substance, enterococcal surface protein [esp], cytolysin, hyaluronidase), and the IS16 marker associated with the clonal complex 17 (CC17) lineage. A total of 231 Enterococcus isolates were recovered, including Enterococcus faecalis (62.3%) and Enterococcus faecium (34.2%). All E. faecalis isolates were susceptible to ampicillin, vancomycin, and linezolid; all E. faecium isolates were resistant to ampicillin, and 7.6% exhibited vanA-mediated glycopeptide resistance. The ermB gene was the predominant macrolide resistance determinant. Among E. faecium, esp (74.7%) was the most prevalent virulence gene, whereas E. faecalis mainly harbored gelE (78.5%). The IS16 element, characteristic of CC17 clones, was detected in 86.1% of E. faecium isolates. The present study highlights the emergence of multidrug-resistant E. faecium strains with molecular features suggestive of CC17 affiliation in hospital settings in Sfax, Tunisia, underscoring the urgent need for stronger infection control and antimicrobial stewardship programs.

Molecular Insights and Therapeutic Potential of Benzothiazole Derivatives: A Comprehensive Pharmacological Review
abstract: Benzothiazole (BTA), a fused bicyclic heterocycle of thiazole and benzene units, has become a special scaffold for medicinal chemistry with a vast pharmacological profile. Structural modification at the benzothiazole core provides enormous flexibility toward rationalizing bioactivity in a wide range of therapeutics. Contemporary research is exemplified by benzothiazole derivatives as potent antibacterial agents, efficiently targeting multidrug-resistant pathogens by mechanisms like DNA gyrase inhibition and membrane disruption. They also exhibit multi-target-directed ligand- based anti-Alzheimer's activity by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase, monoamine oxidases, and β-secretase enzymes. In cancer, benzothiazole hybrids are found to be selectively cytotoxic toward different cancer cell lines, such as breast, lung, and liver cancers, and are generally more active than the traditional drugs. Anti-tubercular activity presents superior inhibition of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, including, Multidrug-resistance (MDR) and Extensively Drug- Resistance (XDR), by novel hybrid conjugates and heterocyclic linkages. Additionally, benzothiazole analogues exhibit anti-inflammatory and anti-diabetic activity with cyclooxygenase, Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 (DPP-4), α-glucosidase, and α-amylase enzyme inhibitory activity. Structure-Activity Relationship (SAR) analysis consistently indicates that electron-withdrawing or electron-donating functions, linker type, and heteroatom position in modulating pharmacological activity. Recent patents reflect sustained innovation in drug design with the benzothiazole motif, and therapeutic applications exist in antimicrobial, anticancer, neuroprotection, and metabolic disorders. Overall, these findings place emphasis on benzothiazole derivatives as highly effective lead templates with immense therapeutic value, warranting further consideration towards clinical usefulness.

title: The influence of antibiotic perturbation on methane oxidation from the perspective of cross-media coupling: Effects, mechanisms and prospects
abstract: Methane oxidation represents a vital biological sink for mitigating methane emissions and climate warming. However, the responses of methane oxidation to antibiotic exposure, together with the associated ecological consequences, remain insufficiently understood. This review synthesizes current evidence on the environmental consequences of antibiotic-induced perturbations to methane oxidation and the mechanisms underlying these effects across multiple scales and environmental compartments, including soils, freshwater sediments, estuarine wetlands, aquaculture sediments, and biofilms in constructed wetlands. Particular attention is given to aerobic methane oxidation and denitrifying anaerobic methane oxidation, with antibiotic effects evaluated at the molecular, physiological, microbial-community, and ecosystem levels. At the cellular level, antibiotics may interfere with particulate methane monooxygenase activity and induce reactive oxygen species-mediated oxidative stress, whereas dose- and exposure-duration-dependent effects may produce low-dose stimulation, high-dose inhibition, or other non-monotonic response patterns. At broader ecological scales, these direct effects are further modulated by antibiotic-induced changes in redox conditions, nitrogen and sulfur cycling, microbial community composition, microbial interaction networks, and antibiotic resistance gene enrichment; collectively, these changes reshape methane oxidation capacity. Available evidence therefore indicates strong environmental-compartment dependence, process specificity, and dose-time dependence in the response of methane oxidation to antibiotic exposure. By altering the balance between methane production and consumption, these perturbations may ultimately modify net methane fluxes and thereby generate additional feedbacks to climate warming. This review provides a mechanistic framework for understanding antibiotic-induced perturbations of methane oxidation, identifies priorities for future research, and supports the integration of methane-cycle responses into ecological risk assessment and environmental management across diverse environmental compartments.
